text: Throughout this article, we use the following notations:

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
text:
1 Background

Proposition 1 For any random variable X, we have 
    X = F_X^{-1}(U).



Proof. For any x, we have 
    P(X \le x) = F_X(x) = P(U \le F_X(x)) = P(F_X^{-1}(U) \le x).
 Thus X = F_X^{-1}(U).

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
section: 2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
text:
2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
Now, we want to perform uniform sampling on the unit disk. We use polar coordinates; more specifically, we take r\cos(\theta), r\sin(\theta), where

r \in [0,1] such that P(r) \propto r (\Rightarrow P(r) = 2r)
\theta \sim U(0,2\pi)

The key lies in 1., that is, how to sample r such that P(r) = 2r. Let X be the random variable such that P(X = r) = 2r. Then, F_X(x) = \int_0^x 2r\,dr = x^2, and thus F_X^{-1}(y) = \sqrt{y}.

2.1 Code
With above in mind, we sample 10000 points on the unit disk, see Figure 1.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Sample the points
N = 10000
inv_cdf = lambda x: np.sqrt(x)
R = np.vectorize(inv_cdf)(np.random.uniform(0, 1, N))
T = np.random.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, N)
points = [(r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)) for r, t in zip(R, T)]

# 2. Make a scatter plot
x, y = zip(*points)
plt.scatter(x, y, s=1)
plt.xticks([])
plt.yticks([])
ax = plt.gca()
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['bottom'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['left'].set_visible(False)
plt.show()








Figure 1: Sampling 10000 points uniformly on the unit disk.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
On the pitch ruler
In this ideal model, an open string’s frequencies sit exactly on the lines: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. Each stem’s height is how far that mode still swings a quarter of a second after the pluck. Touch at the middle and the odd stems die almost at once; what is left sits on every second line, the lines of a note twice as high. Touch at a third and only every third stem survives. Move the pluck point too: near the bridge the stems shrink slowly as they go up, and at the middle they shrink fast, with every second stem missing even without a finger.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
How it works
Tied ends keep half of the loop’s waves. A string tied at both ends can only take shapes that stay still at the ends: one arch, two arches, three, …. Each is exactly half of a wave on a loop twice as long, so the reason from page 3 still holds (a shorter wave bends more sharply, and the string pulls back in proportion to how sharply it bends): a shape with n arches is n times shorter, is pulled back n² times harder, and swings n times faster. The frequencies are exactly 1, 2, 3, … times the lowest, which itself rises with the tension and falls with the string’s length and its weight per length. One thing does change: on a loop each frequency had two waves, one shifted along the loop; on a string a wave cannot run around, it reflects at the ends, and each frequency has a single shape, a standing wave.



Step-by-step derivationThe string’s operator and its frequencies uses derivatives and integration by parts

The operator and its boundary condition. A string of length L, tension T and mass \mu per unit length obeys the wave equation, derived on the circle page: 
u_{tt} = -c^2 A u, \qquad A = -\frac{d^2}{dx^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}, \qquad u(0) = u(L) = 0 .
 The same rule -d^2/dx^2 now acts on shapes on the interval [0, L], and only shapes that vanish at both ends are allowed. That restriction, called a Dirichlet condition, changes which shapes are eigenfunctions, and so changes the spectrum. An operator is the rule together with the shapes it is allowed to act on. As on the circle page, the operator proper is c^2A, and we work with A.
Spectrum. The solutions of -X'' = k^2X are a\cos kx + b\sin kx. The condition X(0) = 0 forces a = 0, and X(L) = 0 then needs \sin kL = 0, so k = n\pi/L. The eigenfunctions are \sin(n\pi x/L) for n = 1, 2, 3, \dots, with eigenvalues (n\pi/L)^2, and the frequencies are 
f_n = \frac{c\,k_n}{2\pi} = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} .
 Exactly whole-number multiples of f_1, as on the circle. (There are no other eigenvalues. Multiply -X'' = \lambda X by X and integrate by parts, using X = 0 at both ends: \lambda\int X^2\,dx = \int (X')^2\,dx. So a zero or negative \lambda would need \int (X')^2\,dx \le 0, which only X = 0 satisfies.) Each eigenvalue now has multiplicity 1, not 2: a wave running along the string reflects at the ends instead of going around, and each reflected pair forms one standing wave.





ProofThe string is half of a circle: the sine series as a Fourier series uses Fourier series and the uniqueness of solutions of the wave equation

Take a shape u on [0, L] with u(0) = u(L) = 0. Extend it to [-L, 0] by u(-x) = -u(x), an odd reflection, and then repeat with period 2L. The result is a shape on a loop of circumference 2L.

  
  
  
  
  0L−L
  stringodd reflection


Odd shapes stay odd. If u(x, t) solves the wave equation on the loop, so does -u(-x, t), since two derivatives in x do not change sign under x \mapsto -x. Starting from an odd shape at rest, both are the same solution by uniqueness, so the motion stays odd.
Odd shapes on the loop are exactly string shapes. An odd periodic shape vanishes at 0, because u(0) = -u(0), and at L, because u(L) = u(-L) = -u(L). Conversely every string shape extends this way.
So the string’s eigenfunctions are the loop’s odd eigenfunctions. On a loop of circumference 2L the eigenfunctions are \cos(n\pi x/L) and \sin(n\pi x/L) with eigenvalues (n\pi/L)^2. The odd ones are the sines. Each eigenvalue keeps one of its two eigenfunctions, which is why the multiplicity drops from 2 to 1.

The sine series of a string shape, u = \sum_n b_n\sin(n\pi x/L), is therefore the Fourier series of its odd extension, and everything proved on the circle page carries over. The same trick with an even reflection, u(-x) = u(x), gives the cosines and the condition u'(0) = u'(L) = 0; the next page combines both reflections for air in a tube.





Step-by-step derivationThe same result from beads with the ends tied uses matrices, as on page 2

Put N beads of mass m, spaced h apart, on a thread of tension T, with both ends tied, so u_0 = u_{N+1} = 0. The force on bead j is the one derived on the ring page, so m\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}). The matrix is now the ring’s matrix without its two corner entries: 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & & \\ -1 & 2 & \ddots & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & -1\\ & & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Its eigenvectors are v_j = \sin\big(n\pi j/(N+1)\big), the sampled sines, with eigenvalues 4\sin^2\big(n\pi/(2(N+1))\big) for n = 1, \dots, N. To check: \sin(\alpha(j+1)) + \sin(\alpha(j-1)) = 2\cos\alpha\,\sin(\alpha j), so (Kv)_j = (2 - 2\cos\alpha)\,v_j = 4\sin^2(\alpha/2)\,v_j with \alpha = n\pi/(N+1), and the tied ends hold because \sin 0 = \sin n\pi = 0. As on the ring, letting N \to \infty with L = (N+1)h and \mu = m/h fixed gives the wave equation and the frequencies f_n = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}.


A light touch keeps only the shapes that are still under the finger. Where a shape has a still point, a node, the finger has nothing to grab, and that shape rings on. Every other shape moves under the finger and loses its energy to it within a moment. At the middle, the shapes with a node there are the ones with an even number of arches: 2, 4, 6, …, at 2, 4, 6, … times the open string’s frequency, a note an octave up. At a third, the survivors have 3, 6, 9, … arches: three times the frequency, an octave and a fifth up (a factor 2 times a factor 3/2). (In this simple model the finger drains each shape in proportion to how much that shape moves under it, the rule the piano page derives for felt dampers.)



PreciselyWhich modes survive a light touch uses the sine function

Let the finger touch the string at the distance s from the nut, and write X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L) for the shape of mode n. In the model, the finger drains mode n at a rate proportional to X_n(s)^2, how much that mode moves under it. The modes that survive are the ones with a node right under the finger: \sin(n\pi s/L) = 0, which means ns/L is a whole number. At s = L/2 these are the even n, at 2f_1, 4f_1, 6f_1, \dots: a note with fundamental 2f_1. At s = L/3 they are n = 3, 6, 9, \dots, with fundamental 3f_1: an octave (a factor 2) and a fifth (a factor 3/2) up, since 2 \times 3/2 = 3.


Where you pluck sets the brightness. A pluck starts each shape according to how much of it is in the plucked triangle. What reaches your ear is the string’s push on the bridge, and for the same height a shape with more arches has steeper ends, so it pushes harder. Pluck near the bridge, and the first several shapes push the bridge about equally hard (near the end, a shape with n arches starts about 1/n as large but is n times as steep, so the pushes come out about equal; fold below): the sound is bright. Pluck at the middle, and every shape with an even number of arches is missing, since those stand still exactly where you pulled; the rest push the bridge less and less, the more arches they have: a mellow, hollow sound.



Step-by-step derivationHow much of each shape a pluck starts uses integration by parts

By the circle page, every shape of the string is a sum \sum_n b_n\sin(n\pi x/L) of its modes, and b_n says how much of mode n the shape contains. A string pulled aside a distance d at a point x_p from one end, and let go, starts as a triangle. With x_p measured from the nut, where x = 0, its sine coefficients are 
b_n = \frac{2dL^2}{\pi^2 x_p(L - x_p)}\cdot\frac{\sin(n\pi x_p/L)}{n^2}.
 Measuring x_p from the bridge instead only flips the sign of every second b_n, since \sin(n\pi(L - x_p)/L) = \pm\sin(n\pi x_p/L), and signs do not change how loud a mode is; from here on x_p is the distance from the bridge. What reaches your ear is driven by the force on the bridge, which is proportional to the string’s slope there and so to n\,b_n for mode n. Near the bridge, x_p small, \sin(n\pi x_p/L) \approx n\pi x_p/L for the first several modes, so n b_n hardly falls off at all: the high modes are strong and the sound is bright. At the middle, \sin(n\pi/2) is zero for every even n, and the rest have n b_n falling like 1/n: a mellower, hollow sound.
Where the formula comes from. Take L = 1 and write q = x_p. The starting shape is u_0(x) = dx/q for 0 \le x \le q and u_0(x) = d(1 - x)/(1 - q) for q \le x \le 1. Its sine coefficients are b_n = 2\int_0^1 u_0(x)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx, by the perpendicularity of the sines, which the string inherits from the circle page (second fold above). Integrate by parts twice on each straight piece. Since u_0 vanishes at both ends and u_0'' = 0 on each piece, the only term left comes from the jump in slope at the corner, from d/q just left of it to -d/(1-q) just right of it: b_n = \frac{2}{n^2\pi^2}\big(\tfrac{d}{q} + \tfrac{d}{1-q}\big)\sin(n\pi q) = \frac{2d\sin(n\pi q)}{n^2\pi^2 q(1-q)}. The 1/n^2 comes from that single corner.


Pressing down makes a new end. Pressing a finger firmly onto the fingerboard is different: it ties the string down there, and only the piece between the finger and the bridge sounds. A shorter string sounds higher: two-thirds of the length sounds a fifth up, half the length an octave up, and the semitone positions bunch closer together toward the bridge. Play a whole violin: press and hold a string to bow it, slide sideways to finger it, or switch to plucking.


  
  
    Bow (hold)Pizzicato, plucked (tap)
     Wooden body
    Press and hold a string. Slide left and right to finger it.
  
  
  Left edge: the nut; right edge: the bridge. Ticks: where the finger goes for each semitone (fold below). Stems: the partials you hear; switching the body off or on changes their heights, never their positions.





DetailsWhere the finger goes for each semitone uses powers

The nut is the end of the string near the tuning pegs, and an open string is one not pressed down by a finger. With the finger at distance s from the nut, the vibrating length shrinks to L - s, so the pitch rises by the factor L/(L - s). In equal temperament the twelve semitones of an octave are equal ratios of frequency, so each is 2^{1/12}, and k semitones are 2^{k/12}. Solving L/(L - s) = 2^{k/12} gives s_k = (1 - 2^{-k/12})L: the semitone positions bunch together toward the bridge. These are the ticks on the violin’s fingerboard above.


The bow locks the note. A bow grips the string, drags it along until the string’s pull tears it free, lets it slip back, and grips it again, once per period. By 1860 Hermann von Helmholtz had watched this through a vibration microscope: the string forms two straight pieces joined by one sharp corner, which races between the bridge and the finger. This is Helmholtz motion. It repeats exactly, so its partials sit exactly on the lines. That matters because a real string is slightly stiff, and its own frequencies run a little sharp of the lines (page 7): plucked, each mode rings at its own slightly sharp frequency and fades; bowed, the stick and slip lock the whole motion into exact repetition. The locking comes from the bow’s friction, which is not linear; this page shows it but does not derive it.


    
    BowedPlucked at 1/4
    
    Slowed about 500 times. The faint lens-shaped outline is the path the corner traces. Stems: the partials of the push on the bridge.
  




Step-by-step derivationHelmholtz motion as a sum of modes uses the plucked-string formula above

A vibration microscope’s lens rides on a vibrating tuning fork, so that a bright speck on the string traces a pattern revealing its motion. Helmholtz reported what he saw in 1860 and in his 1863 book. The expansion of Helmholtz motion in the string’s eigenfunctions is, for some overall size a, 
u(x,t) = \sum_{n\ge1} \frac{a}{n^2}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\sin(2\pi n f_1 t).
 Where this comes from: at each moment the string is two straight pieces, like a plucked string, with the corner at some point x_c. Helmholtz showed that the corner’s height is proportional to x_c(L - x_c), so it traces two arcs of a parabola, the lens in the demo, and that the corner moves at the wave speed c = 2Lf_1. Put that height in place of d in the pluck formula above: the factor x_c(L - x_c) cancels and b_n \propto \sin(n\pi x_c/L)/n^2. With x_c = 2Lf_1t this is \sin(2\pi nf_1t)/n^2; on the way back the corner runs along the lower arc, and the same formula covers it: for x_c between L and 2L, \sin(n\pi x_c/L) describes a corner at 2L - x_c with negative height. The motion repeats exactly every 1/f_1 seconds, so its partials sit exactly on nf_1. The force on the bridge is proportional to the string’s slope there, and the slope of \sin(n\pi x/L) carries an extra factor n\pi/L, so partial n pushes the bridge with strength proportional to 1/n. On an ideal string a pluck also gives exact multiples of f_1; the difference between plucking and bowing shows only on a real, slightly stiff string, as described above.


The body changes loudness, not pitch. The string itself moves very little air. It rocks the bridge, the bridge shakes the wooden body, and the body moves the air. Each step is linear: shaken at one frequency, it responds at that same frequency, only louder or quieter and a little delayed. So the body can change each partial’s height but can never move it to another frequency. Toggle the wooden body on the violin above: the stems change height and stay where they are.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
What we found
Tying a string’s ends down keeps half of the loop’s waves, so its frequencies still land exactly on the lines. A light touch drains every wave that moves under the finger, so only those already still there survive: at the middle, every second one, which is a note an octave up. And the operator lesson: the rule for what the ends may do, a boundary condition, is part of the operator. It decides which shapes are allowed, and so which frequencies.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
On the pitch ruler
Here are both drums’ first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest: 1×, 1.20×, 1.43×, 1.60×, 1.69×, 1.90×, 2.04×, …. Like the drum on page 8, they sit off the gray whole-number lines, so neither drum has a clear pitch. And the two lists are the same to every digit computed: the stems under drum A and drum B stand in the same places. Each stem’s height is how strongly a strike at the clicked point starts that mode: all equal until you click, then different on the two drums, because it depends on the mode’s shape at the struck point.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
How it works
A list of frequencies comes from a list of eigenvalues. In the series’ language: on page 8 the drumhead became an operator, a rule that turns a shape of the drumhead into the force pulling it back toward rest. Its eigenvalues give the drum’s frequencies, and its eigenfunctions are the mode shapes. Kac’s question asks whether the frequencies alone, with nothing about the mode shapes, fix the shape of the drumhead.



PreciselyKac’s question in symbols uses the Laplacian (page 8)

A drum’s operator, from the drum page, is -c^2\Delta on the drumhead \Omega, a bounded region of the plane in one piece, with u = 0 on the rim. Here \Delta is the Laplacian. Write \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \lambda_3 \le \cdots for the eigenvalues of -\Delta, each repeated as many times as it occurs (its multiplicity). The drum’s frequencies are then f_k = \frac{c}{2\pi}\sqrt{\lambda_k}. Kac’s question, in these terms, is whether the list \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots determines the shape of \Omega. Kac wrote that he had first heard the question posed this way about ten years earlier, from Salomon Bochner.


The list knows the area and the length of the rim. Count how many of a drum’s frequencies lie below some limit. As the limit rises, the count grows in proportion to the drum’s area: twice the area, about twice as many modes below any high limit. This is Weyl’s law, from 1911, so the area can be heard. The count also falls short of the area’s share, by an amount in proportion to the length of the rim: holding the rim still costs the drum some modes. (Proved, in a slightly smoothed form, for every rim that is smooth or made of straight pieces; the fold has the details.) The demo counts the frequencies of three drums with the same area: once the area’s share, the same for all three, is taken away, the drum with the longest rim sits lowest.


  
  
    Modes below the limit
    Minus the area's share
  
  Frequency limit
  
  Three drums of equal area: a disk, a square, a long rectangle. Steps: the true counts. Dashed: Weyl's formula, area and rim together. Gray: the area's share alone, the same for all three.





PreciselyWeyl’s law and the rim term uses limits

Count the eigenvalues up to \lambda: N(\lambda) = \#\{k : \lambda_k \le \lambda\}, where \# means “the number of”. For large \lambda, 
N(\lambda) \approx \frac{A}{4\pi}\,\lambda \;-\; \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt{\lambda},
 where A is the area of the drum and P the length of its rim, and “\approx” means that the error, divided by \sqrt\lambda, shrinks to zero as \lambda grows. The first term is Weyl’s law. Hermann Weyl proved it in 1911, and later work extended it to every drum. So the area can be heard: it is 4\pi times the rate at which N grows. In the demo all three drums have area \pi (a disk of radius 1, a square, and a rectangle 4 times as long as it is wide), so the area’s share is \lambda/4, and “minus the area’s share” plots N(\lambda) - \lambda/4, roughly -P\sqrt\lambda/4\pi: the longer the rim, the lower the curve. The demo’s frequency limit is shown as a multiple of the disk’s lowest frequency, \sqrt{\lambda/\lambda_1}.
The second term is subtler. Weyl conjectured it, and Victor Ivrii proved it in 1980 for drums with smooth rims, provided that closed billiard paths are rare. A billiard path is the path of a ball rolling inside the drum and bouncing off the rim, angle in equal to angle out; it is closed if it comes back to where it started, heading the same way. “Rare” means that if you pick a starting point and a direction at random, the chance of landing on a closed path is zero. Ivrii conjectured that this always holds; it has not been proved. The square and the rectangle in the demo have corners, which his theorem does not cover, but for them the formula can be checked by counting, as in the next fold. The perimeter can be heard in any case, for every drum whose rim is smooth or a polygon, by a smoother way of counting; that is the fold after it.





Proof sketchWeyl’s law for a square, by counting dots uses partial derivatives

Take the square of side s. Its eigenfunctions are \sin(m\pi x/s)\sin(n\pi y/s) for whole numbers m, n \ge 1, with eigenvalues (\pi/s)^2(m^2 + n^2); substituting them into the equation checks this, as for the circle on page 3. So N(\lambda) is the number of dots (m, n), with m, n \ge 1, inside the quarter circle of radius R = s\sqrt\lambda/\pi.















RR

Give each dot the unit square centered on it. These squares nearly fill the quarter disk, which has area \pi R^2/4. What they miss is a strip of width \tfrac12 along each axis, of area about R/2 each, shaded in the figure; the squares sticking out past the arc and the gaps inside it roughly cancel. So 
N(\lambda) \approx \frac{\pi R^2}{4} - R = \frac{s^2}{4\pi}\lambda - \frac{4s}{4\pi}\sqrt\lambda = \frac{A}{4\pi}\lambda - \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt\lambda .
 In the figure, R = 5.3: there are 17 dots, and the formula gives 16.8. The strips are missing because m = 0 and n = 0 give the zero function, not an eigenfunction: the rim’s condition u = 0 is what costs the perimeter term. Making “roughly cancel” precise is a classical problem about counting lattice points in a circle.





Proof sketchHearing the perimeter of any drum: a smoother count uses the heat equation and the reflection trick of page 4

N(\lambda) jumps by one at every eigenvalue, and those jumps can bunch up, which is what Ivrii’s condition controls. A smoother count avoids them. For t > 0 let 
Z(t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}.
 Each eigenvalue adds nearly 1 if \lambda_k is much less than 1/t and nearly 0 if it is much more, so Z(t) is roughly N(1/t), with the jumps smoothed out. Like N, Z is determined by the list of eigenvalues.
Z has a physical meaning. Heat spreading on the drumhead, with the rim held at temperature 0, obeys v_t = \Delta v, the drum’s equation with one time derivative instead of two, so each mode now decays like e^{-\lambda_k t} instead of oscillating. Start a unit burst of heat at a point x and let it spread for time t. The temperature it leaves at x itself, added up over all points x of the drum, is Z(t). (Write the burst as a sum of modes, each scaled so that \iint X_k^2\,dA = 1. A burst at x contains mode k in proportion to X_k(x), the same rule as a strike on the drum page; after time t that part has shrunk by e^{-\lambda_k t}, and its temperature at x is again proportional to X_k(x). So the temperature left at x is \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}X_k(x)^2, and adding it up over the drum gives \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}.) In a short time t heat travels a distance of about \sqrt t, so a burst only feels the rim if it starts within about that distance of it. Kac called this “not feeling the boundary”. Then:

Away from the rim, the burst spreads as on an endless plane, and the temperature it leaves at its starting point is 1/(4\pi t). Adding this up over the drum gives A/(4\pi t).
Near a straight piece of rim, at distance r from it, the rim’s condition v = 0 is met by adding a mirror-image burst of opposite sign on the far side of the rim, the odd reflection of the string page. The image is a distance 2r away, and lowers the temperature at x by e^{-r^2/t}/(4\pi t). Adding this up over a strip along the rim, using \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/t}\,dr = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi t} for each unit of rim length, gives -P/(8\sqrt{\pi t}).

So, as t \to 0, 
Z(t) = \frac{A}{4\pi t} - \frac{P}{8\sqrt{\pi t}} + (\text{terms that stay bounded}).
 Knowing Z, one reads off A from the first term and then P from the second. Kac gave this argument in his 1966 paper. Åke Pleijel had already proved the formula for smooth rims in 1954, by another method; Henry McKean and Isadore Singer proved in 1967 the next, constant term, which Kac had conjectured, from an argument that was not a full proof: (1 - h)/6 for a drum with h holes and a smooth rim; and Michiel van den Berg and Sivakolundu Srisatkunarajah proved the formula for polygons in 1988. Unlike N, Z needs no condition on billiard paths, because averaging over a range of eigenvalues smooths out the bunching.


So a round drum can be heard. Of all shapes with the same area, the disk has the shortest rim. Both the area and the rim’s length can be heard, so a drum, with a smooth or straight-sided rim, that has exactly a disk’s frequencies has the disk’s area and the disk’s rim length, and so it must be a disk. Kac pointed this out in his 1966 paper: “By pitch alone one can thus determine whether a drum is circular or not!”



PreciselyThe disk argument in symbols uses the isoperimetric inequality

The isoperimetric inequality says that every drum satisfies P^2 \ge 4\pi A, with equality only for the disk. Both sides can be heard, by the folds above. So a drum, with a smooth or polygonal rim, that has exactly the frequencies of a disk has the disk’s area and perimeter, so P^2 = 4\pi A, so it is a disk. Kac makes this remark in section 10 of his 1966 paper.


But in general, no. Two years before Kac’s paper, John Milnor had found two different shapes with the same frequencies, and Kac said so; but they were 16-dimensional and had no rim. (They are flat tori: 16-dimensional versions of a video-game screen whose edges wrap around, so that leaving on the right brings you back on the left.) For drums in the plane the question stayed open for 26 years. In 1992 Carolyn Gordon, David Webb and Scott Wolpert answered it: no. They found two different polygons with exactly the same frequencies, repeats included: the two drums at the top of this page. Such drums are called isospectral. Since area and rim length can be heard, they must share them, and they do: each is made of seven copies of the same right triangle, with two short sides of length 1, so each has area 3.5 and rim length 6 + 3\sqrt2.
Why do they share every frequency? Cut each drum into its seven triangles. Any mode of drum A can be rebuilt on drum B: fill each of B’s triangles with three triangle-shaped pieces of the mode, taken from A’s triangles, turned or flipped to fit, some with their signs reversed. With the right recipe, the pieces join smoothly across every seam and stay still on B’s rim, so the result is a mode of B, at the same frequency. The recipe runs backwards too, so the two drums have exactly the same frequencies, with the same number of modes at each.



DetailsTransplantation: carrying a mode from one drum to the other uses the Laplacian (page 8)

Cut each drum along its seams into its seven triangles. Take any eigenfunction X of drum A, with eigenvalue \lambda. On each triangle of drum B, place a sum of three pieces of X, each taken from one of A’s triangles, turned or reflected to fit, and some with a minus sign. Each piece satisfies -\Delta X = \lambda X, so the sum does too, inside each triangle. With the right choice of pieces and signs, the result is zero on B’s rim, and across every seam of B both its values and its slopes match. A function that satisfies the equation on both sides of a line, with values and slopes matching on the line, satisfies it across the line too, a standard fact about this equation. At the points where several seams meet, one more standard fact closes the gap: a solution that stays bounded around a single point, and satisfies the equation everywhere near it except possibly at the point itself, satisfies it there too. So the result is an eigenfunction of B with the same \lambda. The construction can be reversed, so each eigenvalue has the same multiplicity on both drums.
This argument is called transplantation. It grew out of work of Peter Buser on surfaces in the 1980s and of Pierre Bérard around 1992; the version for drums like these is in a 1994 paper of Buser, John Conway, Peter Doyle and Klaus-Dieter Semmler. The seven formulas, with pictures, are in Cleve Moler’s blog post on transplantation, and in S. J. Chapman’s article, which does the same by folding paper. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert’s own proof used a method of Toshikazu Sunada from 1985 for building isospectral spaces from group theory; Wikipedia has an overview.





DetailsHow the numbers on this page were computed uses matrices, as on page 2

Each drum is covered by a square grid of spacing h, and the Laplacian is replaced by its five-point version: at each grid point, the sum of the four neighbors minus four times the point, divided by h^2. This is the bead model of page 2 in two dimensions. Grid points on the rim are held at zero. The drums’ corners sit on grid points, so whether each point is inside, on the rim, or outside is decided with exact whole-number arithmetic.
At h = 1/40 and h = 1/80 the two drums give the same first twelve eigenvalues to a relative difference of 3\times10^{-14}, which is rounding error. This is expected, as far as I can tell, because the grid lines up with every triangle’s edges, so transplantation works for the grid model too; Moler’s post transplants grid eigenvectors in the same way. Combining the two grids (Richardson extrapolation) gives values within 0.03% of the high-accuracy values in Table 3.1 of Driscoll’s paper, after multiplying his by 4: his drums are twice the size of these. That is a check, not a precise computation: Richardson’s trick assumes the grid error shrinks like h^2, and the drums’ inward-pointing corners slow that down. The page uses Driscoll’s values.
One eigenvalue is known exactly, the ninth. Its mode is, on each triangle, that triangle’s own lowest mode, \sin\pi x\,\sin 2\pi y - \sin 2\pi x\,\sin\pi y in coordinates where the triangle has corners (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1), with its sign flipping across each seam. Substituting gives the eigenvalue \pi^2(1 + 4) = 5\pi^2 = 49.348\ldots, and Driscoll’s value agrees to every digit he gives. On the grid, the ninth eigenvalue equals the grid version of this mode’s eigenvalue to rounding error, a second check.
The scripts are gww.py for the eigenvalues and gww_modes.py for the mode pictures. The corner coordinates are those in Moler’s first post. The mode pictures use the coarser grid h = 1/40, sampled every 0.1.


Same frequencies, not the same sound. A struck drum’s sound is a sum of its modes, each at its own frequency and with a strength that depends on where it is struck and where it is heard. The two drums share the frequencies. The mode shapes differ, so the strengths from a strike at a given point differ, and so does the timbre, the color of the sound. What the drums share is the answer to “which frequencies can this drum make”, which is exactly what the spectrum records.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
What we found
A drum’s list of frequencies knows its area and the length of its rim, and for a round drum that pins down the shape. In general it does not: two differently shaped drums can share every frequency. On the pitch ruler, both drums are off the lines, like the ideal drumhead of page 8, and in exactly the same places. Every earlier page went from an instrument to its spectrum; this one went backwards, asking what the spectrum says about the instrument. The study of such questions is called spectral geometry.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
How it works
Each bead is pulled toward its neighbors. The string on each side of a bead pulls along itself. When the bead sits above both neighbors, the two pulls together point down, and the further it sits above their average, the harder it is pulled back. So each bead is a mass on a spring, except that where its spring pulls it depends on where its neighbors are.



Step-by-step derivationThe force on one bead uses derivatives and a small-angle approximation

Let u_j be the height of bead j, with beads spaced h apart along a string of tension T, each of mass m. Because the loop closes, bead N is next to bead 1, so indices are counted around the ring. (This is an idealization: a real loop of string would need something to hold it out against its own tension. The model keeps only the sideways pulls between neighbors, exactly as for a straight string whose two ends are joined.) For small displacements, Newton’s law for bead j is 
m\,\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}\left(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}\right).


  
  
  
  
  
  bead j−1bead jbead j+1
  TTnet pull


The string between beads j and j+1 pulls bead j along itself with force T.
Its slope is (u_{j+1} - u_j)/h. Let \theta be the angle that piece of string makes with the horizontal. For small slopes the vertical part of the pull is T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = T(u_{j+1} - u_j)/h.
The string on the other side contributes T(u_{j-1} - u_j)/h.
Adding the two and applying Newton’s law gives the equation above. The bracket u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1} is twice the gap between the average of the neighbors and bead j itself: a bead sitting above its neighbors is pulled down, one sitting below is pulled up.

The assumptions are small slopes and a tension that does not change as the string flexes.


Some shapes keep their shape. Most starting shapes change as they move: that is the tangle. But in a few special shapes, every bead is pulled back in proportion to its own height, by the same factor for every bead. Then every bead is a mass on the same spring, they all swing in step, and the shape only grows and shrinks. That is a mode, with one frequency. And any motion, even the tangle, is a sum of modes, each swinging on its own: a chord.
In the series’ language, write all the heights as one list. The pulls on all the beads come from one table of numbers, a matrix, applied to that list: the ring’s operator. A mode’s shape is an eigenvector of the matrix, a list that the matrix only rescales; the rescaling factor is its eigenvalue, and the mode’s frequency goes as its square root. The list of all the eigenvalues is the matrix’s spectrum.



Step-by-step derivationThe matrix, its eigenvectors, and why each one is a mode uses matrices

The matrix. Collect the heights into a column u = (u_1, \dots, u_N). The equations for all beads at once read \ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}\,K u, where K is the N\times N matrix with 2 on the diagonal, -1 just above and below it, and -1 in the two corners, because bead 1 and bead N are neighbors. For N = 5, 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Here Ku is the column whose j-th entry is row j of K times u: multiply each entry of row j by the matching entry of u, and add. Row j has 2 in place j and -1 in places j - 1 and j + 1, so (Ku)_j = 2u_j - u_{j-1} - u_{j+1}, and the matrix equation is the bead equation for every bead at once. Each row of K is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around; a matrix with this property is called circulant.
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues. A nonzero column v is an eigenvector of K, with eigenvalue \lambda, if Kv = \lambda v: the matrix only rescales it, possibly by zero. The set of all eigenvalues is the spectrum of K.
Modes. If Kv = \lambda v, then u(t) = v\cos(\omega t) is a motion of the beads, provided \omega^2 = \frac{T}{mh}\lambda. To check, differentiate twice: \ddot u = -\omega^2 v\cos\omega t, while -\frac{T}{mh}Ku = -\frac{T}{mh}\lambda v\cos\omega t. Every bead swings at the same angular frequency \omega (radians per second; page 1), in the fixed shape v. This is the mass on a spring again, once for each eigenvector.
A small example, three beads. For N = 3, 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Row j of this K gives (Kv)_j = 3v_j - (v_1 + v_2 + v_3). The column (1, 1, 1) gives K(1,1,1) = (0,0,0), so it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0: every bead moves up together, nothing stretches, nothing pulls back, and the frequency is 0, so the ring just drifts. Any column whose entries add up to zero gives (Kv)_j = 3v_j, so Kv = 3v. Every such column is a combination a(1, -1, 0) + b(0, 1, -1), so these eigenvectors fill a whole plane: every one is built from those two shapes, and neither of the two is a multiple of the other. The eigenvalues are 0, 3, 3, with 3 counted twice: it has multiplicity 2.





ProofEvery motion is a sum of modes uses linear algebra

The matrix K is symmetric: the entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. By the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, K has a basis of N mutually orthogonal (perpendicular) eigenvectors v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(N)} with real eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N. Write the motion as u(t) = \sum_k a_k(t)\,v^{(k)}. Substituting into \ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}Ku and taking the dot product with v^{(k)}, which removes every other term because they are perpendicular, gives \ddot a_k = -\omega_k^2 a_k with \omega_k^2 = \frac{T}{mh}\lambda_k: each coefficient obeys its own mass-on-a-spring equation. With starting shape u(0) = \sum_k c_k v^{(k)} and starting velocity \dot u(0) = \sum_k d_k v^{(k)}, and by the uniqueness of solutions from page 1, every motion is u(t) = \sum_k \big(c_k\cos\omega_k t + \frac{d_k}{\omega_k}\sin\omega_k t\big)v^{(k)}, read as c_k + d_k t when \omega_k = 0. The eigenvalues are nonnegative because u \cdot Ku = \sum_j u_j(2u_j - u_{j+1} - u_{j-1}) = \sum_j (u_{j+1} - u_j)^2 \ge 0, by regrouping the terms around the ring; for an eigenvector this equals \lambda\,(u\cdot u).


The modes are waves around the ring. On a ring no bead is special, so the special shapes are waves that fit a whole number of times around: a wave with one crest, two crests, three, and so on. A wave with more crests bends more sharply from bead to bead, so each bead is pulled back harder and the wave swings faster. In the 1730s Daniel Bernoulli studied systems like this, weights strung along a flexible thread and a hanging chain, and came to believe that every vibration is built from such simple motions; in 1753 he put this forward as a general principle.



Step-by-step derivationThe waves and their eigenvalues, for any number of beads uses trigonometric identities

Try the column v_j = \cos(2\pi jk/N), a wave with k crests around the ring. The identity \cos(a + b) + \cos(a - b) = 2\cos a\cos b, with a = 2\pi jk/N and b = 2\pi k/N, gives v_{j+1} + v_{j-1} = 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\,v_j, so 
(Kv)_j = 2v_j - v_{j+1} - v_{j-1} = \big(2 - 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\big)\,v_j = 4\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi k}{N}\Big)\,v_j ,
 using 1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x. The same holds for v_j = \sin(2\pi jk/N). These are the shapes the mode buttons play, and the eigenvalues are 4\sin^2(\pi k/N). At the beads, a wave with N - k crests looks exactly like one with k crests (the cosine is the same and the sine changes sign), so the different eigenvalues come from k = 0, 1, \dots up to N/2, rounded down, and each one from k = 1 up to just below N/2 has two eigenvectors, a cosine and a sine. (At k = 0, and at k = N/2 when N is even, the sine is zero at every bead, so only the cosine is left.) Writing any motion as a sum of these waves splits it into separate masses on springs, one per wave; that splitting is the discrete Fourier transform.





PreciselyThe same waves, written with complex numbers uses complex numbers

With Euler’s formula e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x, the cosine and sine waves combine into v_j = e^{2\pi i jk/N} for k = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1 (here i is the imaginary unit and j the bead number). Then (Kv)_j = \big(2 - e^{2\pi ik/N} - e^{-2\pi ik/N}\big)v_j = 4\sin^2(\pi k/N)\,v_j in one line. These N waves are the basis vectors of the discrete Fourier transform, and they are eigenvectors of every circulant matrix, not only this one. Combined with the time factor e^{\mp i\omega t}, the waves with k and N - k crests travel around the ring in opposite directions.


Almost whole numbers. A long wave, with few crests, spreads over many beads, and to it the beads look like a smooth string; its frequency grows in step with its number of crests, almost exactly as whole numbers do. A short wave, with crests only a bead or two apart, feels the gaps between the beads, and its frequency falls behind. That is why the low stems sit near the lines and close in as you add beads, while the high ones stay off.



PreciselyHow near to whole numbers uses the sine function

By the eigenvalues above, mode k has angular frequency \omega_k = 2\sqrt{T/(mh)}\,\sin(\pi k/N), so its frequency is proportional to \sin(\pi k/N), which is not proportional to k: the beads are not exactly harmonic. For small k, \sin(\pi k/N) \approx \pi k/N, so the low modes are nearly harmonic, and the ratio \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N) tends to k as N grows. The modes near k = N/2 stay far from the whole-number grid: for an even number of beads the largest ratio is 1/\sin(\pi/N) (slightly less for an odd number), and for any number of beads it is about N/\pi once there are many, not N/2. A mode can land on a line by coincidence: with 6 beads, the top mode sits at exactly 2×.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
What we found
Many coupled masses move in a few special shapes, modes, each swinging at its own frequency like a single mass on a spring, and any motion, even a tangle, is a sum of them: a chord. Finding the modes means finding the special shapes of one matrix, the ring’s operator. On a ring the modes are waves, and the low ones sit near the lines of the pitch ruler, but not on them.

Hold the blow button on the clarinet, then switch the same tube to a flute and blow again. The register key (on the flute it stands in for blowing harder) makes either tube jump to its next mode.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
On the pitch ruler
The stems under the demo are the frequencies in the sound, on a ruler whose gray lines are whole-number multiples of the note being played. The flute’s stems sit on every line. The clarinet’s sit on the lines too, but the strong ones are at 1, 3, 5, 7, …; in the low register (the lowest notes) the even ones are faint. Both sounds are notes. What the closed end changes is which lines are strong, and how low the whole ruler starts.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
How it works
Same equation, other ends. The air in a tube obeys the same wave equation as a string, with the air pressure in place of the string’s sideways displacement and the speed of sound, about 343 m/s, in place of the string’s wave speed (fold below). What differs is the ends. At an open end the air meets the room, so the pressure there stays at room pressure, just as a string’s tied end stays put. At the clarinet’s reed the opening is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move back and forth: it piles up and thins out against the closed end, and the pressure swings most there.



Step-by-step derivationNewton’s law for a slab of air uses partial derivatives


  
  
  
  
  p(x)p(x+dx)
  slab, mass ρS dx


Let \xi(x, t) be how far the air that normally sits at x has moved along the tube, and let the tube’s cross-section have area S.
The slab of air between x and x + dx has mass \rho S\,dx. The only force on it along the tube is the pressure difference between its two faces, S\,[p(x) - p(x + dx)] \approx -S\,p_x\,dx. Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, divided by S\,dx, is \rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x.
The slab’s two faces move by \xi(x) and \xi(x + dx), so its length changes by \xi(x + dx) - \xi(x) \approx \xi_x\,dx: it is stretched by the fraction \xi_x, and its pressure drops in proportion: p = -K\,\xi_x. In a sound wave the squeezing is too fast for heat to flow, which is called adiabatic; for air this makes K about 1.4 times atmospheric pressure.
Differentiate step 2 in x and step 3 twice in t: \rho\,\xi_{ttx} = -p_{xx} and p_{tt} = -K\,\xi_{xtt}. Eliminating \xi gives p_{tt} = (K/\rho)\,p_{xx}.

What was assumed: the tube is narrow compared with the sound’s wavelength, so the pressure is the same across it, and the pressure changes are small. Friction with the walls is left out.


Half a wave or a quarter. The flute’s lowest mode has room pressure at both ends and swings most in the middle: half a wavelength fits in the tube. The clarinet’s lowest mode swings most at the reed and has room pressure at the open end: only a quarter of a wavelength fits. A wave twice as long has half the frequency, so the same ideal tube sounds exactly an octave lower closed at one end. Real flutes and clarinets differ a little in length, the clarinet’s mouthpiece and bell change its effective length, and the open ends act slightly longer than they are, so the real interval comes out a bit less than an octave.



PreciselyThe two end conditions and the two spectra uses derivatives

The operator. Let p(x, t) be the air pressure in the tube minus room pressure. The fold above shows that it obeys the wave equation again, 
p_{tt} = c^2 p_{xx}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{K}{\rho} \approx (343\ \text{m/s})^2,
 where \rho is the density of air and K its bulk modulus, its resistance to being squeezed (this K has nothing to do with the bead matrix of page 2). The constant c is the speed of sound, about 343 m/s at 20 °C. So the operator is again -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, now acting on pressure shapes along the tube.
Boundary conditions. At an open end the air in the tube meets the room, so the pressure there is room pressure: p = 0. This is approximate: the air just outside moves with the air inside, so the tube acts as if it were slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius at each open end, an amount called the end correction. At the clarinet’s reed the opening is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move back and forth. Air that never moves has no acceleration, so the net push on it is zero; that push is set by how fast the pressure changes along the tube, p_x, so p_x = 0 there (step 2 of the fold above, with \xi the air’s displacement along the tube). The first of these is the string’s Dirichlet condition. The second, a condition on the slope, is called a Neumann condition.
Spectrum. A mode is a pressure shape X(x) with -X'' = k^2 X, so X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx, and its frequency is f = ck/2\pi. For the clarinet, X'(0) = bk = 0 at the reed forces b = 0, leaving X = \cos kx, and X(L) = 0 at the open end needs \cos kL = 0, so kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2 and f_n = (2n-1)c/4L. For the flute, open at both ends, the conditions are the string’s, and give \sin(n\pi x/L). So

flute

\sin(n\pi x/L)
f_n = n\,\dfrac{c}{2L}


clarinet
closed, open
\cos\big((2n-1)\pi x/2L\big)
f_n = (2n-1)\,\dfrac{c}{4L}



The lowest frequencies are c/2L and c/4L: a ratio of exactly 2 for the same ideal tube. A real clarinet’s bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine these numbers, not the picture.


Only odd multiples. The flute’s higher modes fit 2, 3, 4, … half waves into the tube, so its modes sit at every whole-number multiple of its lowest. The clarinet’s must keep the pressure swinging most at the reed and at room level at the open end, and that fits 1, 3, 5, … quarter waves, with nothing in between: only odd multiples. So when a clarinetist presses the register key, the tube jumps to 3 times its lowest frequency, an octave and a fifth, called a twelfth (a fifth is the ratio 3/2). A flutist overblows by blowing faster, and the flute’s next mode is 2 times its lowest, an octave. That is why clarinet fingerings repeat a twelfth apart and flute fingerings an octave apart.



ProofWhy only odd multiples: the closed tube is a quarter of a loop uses the circle’s eigenfunctions (page 3)

Use the reflections from the string page. Take a pressure shape p on [0, L] with p_x(0) = 0 and p(L) = 0.

Reflect it evenly across the reed end, p(-x) = p(x). A smooth even shape has zero slope at 0, so even reflection is what the Neumann condition p_x(0) = 0 allows, so the result is a shape on [-L, L] that vanishes at both ends.
Reflect that oddly across x = L, p(2L - x) = -p(x), and repeat. The result is a shape on a loop of circumference 4L.
On that loop the eigenfunctions are \cos(k\pi x/2L) and \sin(k\pi x/2L). Step 1 keeps only cosines. Step 2 needs \cos\big(k\pi(2L - x)/2L\big) = (-1)^k\cos(k\pi x/2L) to equal -\cos(k\pi x/2L), which keeps only odd k.

So the clarinet’s modes are the odd harmonics of a loop four tube-lengths long, which is where both the factor 4 and the odd numbers come from.





DetailsHow the register key picks out the 3× mode

The clarinet’s register key opens a small hole near the top of the tube. An open hole lets air in and out, pulling the pressure there toward room pressure, which spoils the fundamental, a mode that needs pressure variation at that point. For one note in the lower part of the low register (the notes played without the key), the hole sits about a third of the way down the sounding tube, right where that note’s 3f_1 mode has no pressure variation anyway, so the open hole does not disturb that mode (Wolfe). For the other notes the hole is off that point, well off for the lowest and highest notes you play with the key (Wolfe), and a second effect helps: the air in a small hole has mass, and the faster it must move back and forth, the harder it is to move. At the fundamental’s lower frequency it moves more easily, so the hole leaks enough to spoil that mode; at the higher frequency of the 3f_1 mode it moves much less, so the hole acts almost as a plug. Either way the tube jumps to the 3f_1 mode.


Why the sound still lands on every line. The reed is a valve: when the pressure in the mouthpiece drops it closes, and when the pressure rises it opens, so the air column drives the reed that feeds it. In normal playing this settles into a periodic oscillation, a sound that repeats, at a playing frequency close to the tube’s lowest mode. A sound that repeats has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of its repetition rate (page 0), but it may have all of them. So the tube’s modes are odd multiples only, while the clarinet’s sound has even multiples too: weak in the low register (the lowest notes), where no mode of the tube supports them, but not absent.

title: Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?
text:
What we found
On the pitch ruler, both tubes play notes: their sound repeats, so its frequencies sit on the lines. The ends decide which lines are strong and where the ruler starts. The string’s operator also governs the air pressure in a tube, and changing the condition at one end, from “pressure equals the room’s” to “the air cannot move”, halves the lowest frequency and keeps only its odd multiples as modes: 1, 3, 5, … times the speed of sound divided by four tube lengths.

Same operator, other ends. Stopped organ pipes and pan pipes are closed at one end like the clarinet and share its odd-multiples spectrum. Open organ pipes share the flute’s. Oboes and saxophones have cone-shaped tubes instead of cylinders, a different operator, which this series does not cover.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text: Pluck a string and you get a note you could hum. Strike a drum and you get a thud. Both are a stretched piece of material, set shaking. So why do they sound so different?

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The answer in three steps
1. Everything that vibrates has a set of favorite shapes. A string can swing as one arc, as two halves moving in opposite directions, as three thirds, and so on. Each of these shapes, called a mode, swings at its own frequency.
1×2×3×
2. A pluck sets many of them going at once. What you hear is a chord of the modes’ frequencies: the lowest, called the fundamental, and the overtones above it. They are the stems on the ruler above.
3. Whether that chord sounds like one note depends on how the frequencies line up. If they sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, the sound repeats itself many times a second, and the ear hears that repetition rate as the pitch. A string’s modes do exactly that: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. An ideal drumhead’s land at 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, …: a few fall near a line by chance, but no frequency we hear as pitch fits them all. The sound never repeats, and it dies fast: a thud.

The idea behind the whole series. How an instrument is built, stretched and held decides its modes and their frequencies. Put the frequencies you hear on the pitch ruler: on the lines, a note; off the lines, a clang or a thud. More exactly, you hear a note when they all sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch. Each instrument page puts its instrument on the ruler to see which.

The mathematics, in one sentence. Newton’s law turns each instrument into an operator, a rule that takes a shape of the instrument and gives back the force pulling it back toward rest, and the frequencies come from that operator’s spectrum.



PreciselyThe two ideas, stated exactly uses derivatives


An instrument’s frequencies come from the spectrum of an operator. Write the instrument’s motion as u_{tt} = -Au, where u is its shape, u_{tt} its acceleration, and A the operator: minus the restoring force per unit mass, acting on the shapes allowed by how the instrument is held. The shapes A only rescales are the modes; the rescaling factors are its eigenvalues, and their list is the spectrum. Each frequency is the square root of an eigenvalue, divided by 2\pi. The simplest case is a loop of string, where A = -c^2\,d^2/d\theta^2 and writing a shape in its modes is the Fourier series (page 3).
A clear pitch means the frequencies you hear sit at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the pitch range, from a few dozen to a few thousand hertz. That frequency need not be present itself (page 0). Then the sound repeats, or nearly repeats, and the repetition rate is the pitch. What you hear can differ from the spectrum in two ways: some frequencies die almost at once, leaving the rest (the kalimba, page 6), and a steady bow or breath can lock the motion into exact repetition near one of the operator’s frequencies, even when the operator’s overtones are off the lines (the harmonica, page 6b).

Listen to an octave tuned to exactly 2 : 1, then to a stretched one. The slow wobble in loudness is called a beat.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
On the pitch ruler
Here are the frequencies of a piano note, middle C, or the last key you played on the keyboard below. They sit a little sharp of the gray lines, and the higher the partial, the further sharp; the readout gives the shift in cents, hundredths of a semitone. The low partials are so close to the lines that the ear still hears one clear note. Each stem’s height is how strongly the hammer starts that mode; the hammer strikes an eighth of the way along, where the 8th and 16th modes stand still, so those two are nearly silent.


    Partials of the last key
    
    
    Try the soft pedal or the practice mute on the keyboard below: the high stems shrink, but none of them moves.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
How it works
A piano wire is a string and a bar at once. Tension pulls the wire straight, as on a violin, and the steel also resists being bent, as in a kalimba tine. The two restoring forces simply add. Bending resists short wiggles far more than long ones, so it barely touches the fundamental but pushes the high overtones sharp: the string is slightly inharmonic. For a middle C wire, the 10th partial (the fundamental counts as the 1st) sits about a third of a semitone above ten times the fundamental. Short treble strings, thick for their length, are the stiffest.



PreciselyThe wire’s equation and its frequencies uses partial derivatives

The operator. Forces per unit length add. Tension contributes T\,u_{xx}, as for the string, and bending contributes -EI\,u_{xxxx}, as for the kalimba, so with \mu the mass per unit length (density times cross-section area, the \rho S of the kalimba page) 
\mu\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad u_{tt} = -\mathcal{L}u, \quad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4 ,
 with c^2 = T/\mu and \kappa^2 = EI/\mu. Here \partial_x^2 means two derivatives in x, the same as the subscript xx, and \mathcal{L} is this page’s operator, playing the role A played before. Treat the ends as pinned: held in place but free to pivot, so u = 0 and, since a pivot exerts no bending moment and the moment is EI\,u_{xx}, also u_{xx} = 0. Real piano strings are held a little more firmly than that, which shifts the numbers slightly but not the picture.
Spectrum. Pinned ends make \sin(n\pi x/L) an eigenfunction of both terms at once, so here the two operators’ eigenvalues simply add; that is special to pinned ends, where the two operators share their eigenfunctions, and with clamped ends the formula needs a small correction. Substituting gives \omega^2 = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2 k^4 with k = n\pi/L, so 
f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, \qquad B = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{T L^2},
 where f_0 = c/2L is the lowest frequency the same string would have without stiffness. The actual fundamental is f_1 = f_0\sqrt{1 + B}.
The stiffness constant B is small, but it multiplies n^2, so high partials run noticeably sharp: the string is slightly inharmonic. For a middle C wire B is about 4.4\times10^{-4}, and the 10th partial sits about 37 cents sharp of ten times the fundamental; the next fold has the arithmetic. Since I grows like the fourth power of the wire’s diameter and B falls like 1/L^2, short treble strings, thick for their length, are the stiffest.





Step-by-step derivationFrom Newton’s law on a short piece of wire to its frequencies uses partial derivatives

1. One small piece. Follow the stretch of wire between x and x+dx. Its mass is \mu\,dx and its vertical acceleration is u_{tt}, so Newton’s law says \mu\,dx\,u_{tt} equals the net vertical force on it. Two forces act: the pull of tension, and the wire’s resistance to bending.
2. Tension. The rest of the string pulls on each end of the piece with force T, along the string.

  
  
  
  
  
  TT
  xx+dx
  T uₓ(x)curved piece, mass μ dx
  T uₓ(x+dx)

At the right end the pull points along the slope u_x(x+dx), so for small slopes its vertical part is T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = T\,u_x(x+dx). At the left end it is -T\,u_x(x). Together they give T\,[u_x(x+dx) - u_x(x)] \approx T\,u_{xx}\,dx. A curved piece feels a net pull toward its center of curvature; a straight piece feels none.
3. Bending. The wire also resists bending, exactly like the kalimba’s tine. The kalimba page derives the bending force per unit length, -EI\,u_{xxxx}, where E is steel’s Young’s modulus and I = \pi d^4/64 is the second moment of area of a round wire of diameter d.
4. Newton’s law. Adding the two forces gives \mu\,dx\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}\,dx - EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx. Dividing by \mu\,dx, with c^2 = T/\mu and \kappa^2 = EI/\mu, 
u_{tt} = -\mathcal{L}u, \qquad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4 .

5. Ends. The bridge at one end and a metal bearing point at the other hold the wire in place, so u = 0. If they let the wire pivot freely, they exert no moment, so M = EI\,u_{xx} = 0. These are the pinned conditions u = u_{xx} = 0.
6. Spectrum. Try u = \sin(kx)\cos(\omega t) with k = n\pi/L, which satisfies both pinned conditions. Then u_{xx} = -k^2u and u_{xxxx} = k^4u, so the equation becomes -\omega^2 = -c^2k^2 - \kappa^2k^4, that is 
\omega^2 = c^2k^2\Big(1 + \frac{EI}{T}\,k^2\Big) = \Big(\frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big)^2\Big(1 + \frac{\pi^2EI}{TL^2}\,n^2\Big).
 Taking square roots gives f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, with f_0 = c/2L and B = \pi^2EI/TL^2.
7. How big is B? For a middle C wire, roughly d = 1 mm and L = 0.6 m, with steel’s E = 2\times10^{11} Pa and density 7850 kg/m³; a tension of about 610 N then gives middle C. So I \approx 4.9\times10^{-14} m^4 and B \approx 4.4\times10^{-4}. The 10th partial, at 10f_0\sqrt{1 + 100B}, then sits 1200\log_2\sqrt{(1 + 100B)/(1 + B)} \approx 37 cents sharp of ten times the fundamental f_0\sqrt{1 + B}. These numbers are rough; real strings vary.
8. What was assumed. Small slopes; tension unchanged as the wire flexes; the wire’s rotational inertia neglected (Rayleigh’s correction adds a small term); a uniform wire.


Why exact octaves beat. A tuner sets an octave by ear, listening for beats between the lower note’s second partial and the upper note’s fundamental. Two nearly equal frequencies played together beat at a rate equal to their difference. On a stiff wire the lower note’s second partial is a little more than twice its fundamental, so an upper note tuned to exactly twice the fundamental sits just below that partial, and the two beat. The tuner raises the upper note until the beat stops, which makes the octave slightly wider than 2 : 1. Tuners also listen to other pairs, such as the lower note’s fourth partial against the upper note’s second, and stiffness makes it impossible to silence all of them at once, so real tuning is a compromise; tick “Play every partial” in the demo at the top to hear it, as the stretched octave then wobbles too. Repeated across the keyboard, this is stretch tuning: the top of a piano ends up sharp and the bottom flat, compared with equal temperament. On a stiff string, “exactly 2 : 1” lines up the wrong pair of frequencies.



PreciselyHow much wider than 2 : 1 uses square-root approximations

A tuner sets an octave by listening for beats, a slow wobble in loudness, between the lower note’s second partial and the upper note’s fundamental. Beats happen when two nearly equal frequencies add, at a rate equal to their difference. The lower note’s fundamental is f_0\sqrt{1+B} and its second partial is 2f_0\sqrt{1+4B}. Their ratio is 2\sqrt{(1+4B)/(1+B)} \approx 2\,(1 + 2B)(1 - B/2) \approx 2\,(1 + 3B/2), using \sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 + x/2 and 1/\sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 - x/2 for small x: the second partial is more than twice the fundamental by a factor of about 1 + 3B/2. An upper note tuned to exactly twice the fundamental therefore sits a little below that second partial, and the two beat. To silence the beats the tuner raises the upper note until its fundamental matches the lower note’s second partial, which makes the octave slightly wider than 2 : 1. Tuners also listen to other pairs, such as the lower note’s fourth partial against the upper note’s second, and stiffness makes it impossible to silence all of them at once, so real tuning is a compromise. Repeated across the keyboard, this is stretch tuning: compared with equal temperament, in which every semitone is exactly the ratio 2^{1/12}, the top of a piano is tuned sharp and the bottom flat.


Hammer, dampers and pedals: none of them moves a frequency. The frequencies belong to the wire itself, set by its tension and stiffness. The hammer decides how much of each mode starts, and the felt dampers decide how fast each mode dies. Every control a pianist touches does one of these two things; only the tuner’s wrench, which changes the tension, moves the frequencies. You can try them all on the whole piano further down.



DetailsWhat each control changes

The hammer starts each mode in proportion to the mode’s own height where the hammer hits, so a mode that stands still there stays silent. In a simple model, the felt dampers make each mode die at a rate proportional to how much it moves under the felt. The pedals act on one or the other:

Step-by-step derivationThe full string equation, the hammer weights and the damping rates uses integrals of products of modes and a first-order approximation

The operator is only part of the string’s equation. A real string is also pushed by the hammer and loses energy to damping; here f(x,t) is a force, not a frequency: 
\mu\,u_{tt} + b(x,t)\,u_t = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} + f(x,t).

Each term has one job. The operator, T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}, fixes the frequencies and the mode shapes. The forcing f is the hammer, and it fixes how much of each mode is excited. The damping b is the felt dampers plus small internal losses, and it fixes how fast each mode dies. Every control a pianist touches acts on f or on b. Only the tuner’s wrench, which changes T, touches the operator.
Both effects are read off the mode shapes X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L). A hammer blow at x_h gives mode n a weight proportional to X_n(x_h), the mode’s own height at the hammer. The drum on the next page uses the same rule. A damper felt resting on a short stretch W of the string makes mode n’s swing shrink like e^{-\gamma_n t}, and for weak damping (to first order in b, that is, ignoring terms in b^2) the decay rate is 
\gamma_n = \frac{\int_W b\,X_n^2\,dx}{2\mu\int_0^L X_n^2\,dx}.
 A mode is damped in proportion to how much it moves under the felt, and its frequency shifts only by an amount proportional to \gamma_n^2, negligible for weak damping. A mode with a node under the felt barely notices the damper: in the view of the inside of the piano further down, slide the damper to L/8, where the hammer also sits, and the 8th mode, which has a still point there, is not excited and barely damped.
In the table above, the dampers and the sustain pedal change b; the soft pedal and the practice mute change f; only the tuning pin changes the operator.
1. Expand in modes. Write u(x,t) = \sum_n q_n(t)\,X_n(x), with \mathcal{L}X_n = \omega_n^2X_n and the pinned conditions.
2. Project. Substitute into the full equation, multiply by X_m and integrate along the string. The operator is symmetric with these boundary conditions (in fact self-adjoint), by integrating by parts as on the circle page, so the X_n are orthogonal: \int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx = 0 for m \ne n. The acceleration and operator terms collapse to one term each: 
\mu N_m\,(\ddot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m) + \sum_n D_{mn}\,\dot q_n = F_m(t),
 with N_m = \int X_m^2\,dx, D_{mn} = \int b\,X_mX_n\,dx and F_m = \int f\,X_m\,dx.
3. The hammer. The felt touches a short stretch near x_h, so F_m(t) \approx X_m(x_h)\,P(t), where P(t) is the total force. Every mode gets the same push in time, weighted by X_m(x_h): the mode’s own height at the hammer.
4. The damper. If the damping is weak, the cross terms D_{mn} with m \ne n change the answer only at second order. Keeping the diagonal leaves a damped oscillator for each mode, 
\ddot q_m + 2\gamma_m\,\dot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m = 0, \qquad \gamma_m = \frac{D_{mm}}{2\mu N_m},
 whose solution e^{-\gamma_m t}\cos\big(\sqrt{\omega_m^2 - \gamma_m^2}\,t\big) decays at the rate \gamma_m while its frequency moves only by order \gamma_m^2/\omega_m.
5. Honest limits. A real damper is not weak: it stops a note in a fraction of a second. The formula gives the right picture, that modes are damped by how much they move under the felt, but not exact decay times.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
What we found
On the pitch ruler, a piano’s overtones sit slightly sharp of the lines, more so the higher they go: close enough that you hear one clear note, far enough that an exact octave beats. In the series’ language, the piano adds one new idea: operators add. The wire is pulled tight like a string and resists bending like a bar, so its operator, the rule that turns a shape of the wire into the force pulling it back, is the sum of the string’s and the bar’s. The hammer, the dampers and the pedals act on how the modes start and die, and none of them moves a frequency by more than a hair.

Every real string is a little stiff. Guitar and harp strings belong here too, faintly. The piano is where stiffness is large enough to hear, and large enough to change how pianos are tuned.

DetailsGrand pianos: the middle pedal and the two-stage decay

On a grand piano the middle pedal is usually the sostenuto, which holds up only the dampers of keys already down. Most notes have two or three strings, and Weinreich showed that their coupling through the bridge, each string’s motion slightly shaking the others, produces the piano’s two-stage decay: a loud start that fades fast, then a quiet, long aftersound. DetailsWhere the dampers sit: under-damper and birdcage uprights

Where the dampers touch the string matters, because each mode is damped in proportion to its motion under the felt. Close to an end every low mode barely moves, so a damper there hardly damps the bass. In most modern uprights the dampers sit below the hammers, nearer the middle of the string; in older “birdcage” uprights they sat above the hammers, near the end. Piano restorers report that the under-damper design stops the strings better, partly because its dampers are closer to the middle of the string (Sykes). The slider in the view above moves the damper and shows the effect on each mode.





Reader questionWhat does a damper do, and what would a piano without dampers sound like?

Without dampers, releasing a key would do nothing: every string would ring until it died on its own, exactly as if the sustain pedal were always down. On a real piano each key lifts a felt damper off its strings; letting go drops the damper back and stops the note within a fraction of a second. The sustain pedal lifts all the dampers at once, so released notes keep ringing. The keyboard above models both. The top 20 keys have no dampers at all, as on a real piano: those short strings die out quickly by themselves.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
← 0 Note · The Shape of a Sound · Map · 2 Beads →
Start with the simplest thing that vibrates: a mass on a spring. Change how far you pull it, and watch how long each bob takes.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
On the pitch ruler
A mass on a spring has just one frequency, so on the pitch ruler it is a single stem: a pure tone. The readout gives that frequency. The frequency goes as the square root of stiffness over mass: four times the stiffness doubles it, four times the mass halves it, and the size of the pull never enters. A note needs more than one stem; the next page finds where the others come from.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
How it works
The pull is proportional to the stretch. A spring pulled some distance from rest pulls back with a force proportional to that distance: twice as far, twice the pull. This is Hooke’s law. Newton’s law turns force into acceleration, so the mass always accelerates back toward rest, in proportion to how far away it is. The steady back-and-forth that results has exactly one frequency.



Step-by-step derivationNewton’s law, and the one frequency it allows uses derivatives

A spring pulled a distance x from its resting position (for a hanging spring, the position where the spring’s pull balances gravity) pulls back with force -kx; the constant k is the spring’s stiffness. Newton’s second law says force equals mass times acceleration, so 
m\,\ddot x = -k\,x, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \ddot x = -\lambda\,x \quad\text{with}\quad \lambda = k/m .
 Here \ddot x means the second derivative of position with respect to time, the acceleration. Try a steady oscillation x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi). Differentiating twice gives \ddot x = -\omega^2 x, so it solves the equation exactly when \omega^2 = \lambda. The number \omega is the angular frequency, in radians per second. The cosine repeats each time \omega t grows by 2\pi, so one cycle takes 2\pi/\omega seconds, and the motion repeats f = \omega/2\pi times a second: 
f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} .
 The amplitude A and the starting phase \phi are free: they record how you started the motion, and they do not appear in f.


Twice the swing, the same time. Take any motion of the mass and double it: twice as far from rest at every moment. The pull doubles too, so the acceleration doubles, which is exactly what the doubled motion needs. So the doubled motion is also a motion of the mass, and it repeats just as often. Friction shrinks the swing, which is why a note fades, but light friction of the usual kind, proportional to speed, does not make the rate depend on the size of the swing either.
This needs the pull to be exactly proportional to the stretch. Pulled very far, a real spring stops obeying Hooke’s law, and then a bigger swing does change the rate. A string shows a small version of this: a hard pluck stretches it, raising its tension, so the note starts very slightly sharp and settles as it fades (J. O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing). That is why the pitch barely sags, rather than not at all.



ProofEvery motion is of this form, and the pitch cannot depend on amplitude uses the uniqueness of solutions of a differential equation

Every solution is A\cos(\omega t + \phi). The equation \ddot x = -\lambda x is linear: sums and multiples of solutions are solutions. A solution is determined by its starting position x(0) and starting velocity \dot x(0); this is the uniqueness theorem for ordinary differential equations. The functions \cos\omega t and \sin\omega t, with \omega = \sqrt\lambda, are solutions with starting data (1, 0) and (0, \omega). So the solution with data (x_0, v_0) is x_0\cos\omega t + (v_0/\omega)\sin\omega t. By the formula \cos(\omega t + \phi) = \cos\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\sin\phi, this equals A\cos(\omega t + \phi) with A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + (v_0/\omega)^2}, \cos\phi = x_0/A and \sin\phi = -v_0/(\omega A).
Amplitude cannot change the pitch. If x(t) is a solution, so is 2x(t), by linearity, and it has the same period. Real springs stop obeying Hooke’s law when stretched far; then the equation is no longer linear and the frequency does depend on amplitude (anharmonicity). Strings show a small version of this: a hard pluck stretches the string, raising its tension, so the note starts slightly sharp and settles as it fades. For the gentle vibrations of most playing, the linear law holds well.
With friction. A real string also loses energy. Adding a friction force proportional to the velocity, -2m\gamma\,\dot x, gives x = Ae^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega_d t + \phi) with \omega_d = \sqrt{k/m - \gamma^2}, as long as the friction is light (\gamma^2 < k/m); differentiating twice checks it. The swing shrinks, so the motion no longer repeats exactly, but the rate of its swings, \omega_d, still does not depend on A.


In the series’ language. The pull per unit mass is the displacement times one number, the stiffness divided by the mass, with the direction reversed. The rule “multiply by that number” is the operator in its smallest form, and the frequency comes from it: its square root, divided by 2π. On the next page the one number becomes a table of numbers, a matrix, with many frequencies; later, a rule acting on whole shapes. The frequencies always come from the operator’s special numbers, its eigenvalues.



PreciselyThe operator and its one eigenvalue

Write the equation as \ddot x = -\lambda x. The restoring force per unit mass is -\lambda x: multiply the displacement by \lambda and reverse its direction. We call the rule “multiply by \lambda” the operator, and keep the minus sign in the equation. The one allowed angular frequency is \omega = \sqrt\lambda.
On the next page the single displacement x becomes a list of displacements, one per bead, and the number \lambda becomes a matrix. Later it becomes a differential operator acting on shapes. In every case the allowed angular frequencies \omega = 2\pi f are the square roots of the operator’s eigenvalues. The next page defines eigenvalues properly; for one mass there is one eigenvalue, the number \lambda = k/m itself.

title: Why does a fading note stay in tune?
text:
What we found
Newton’s law, with a pull proportional to the stretch, allows exactly one frequency. It is set by the stiffness and the mass, not by how far the mass swings, and that is why a fading note keeps its pitch, very nearly. One mass gives one stem on the pitch ruler; a note needs many.
