title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
← 6 Kalimba · The Shape of a Sound · Map · 7 Piano →
Pluck the reed, then blow it, and compare the stems with the gray whole-number lines.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
On the pitch ruler
Plucked, the reed’s overtones sit at 6.27× and 17.55×, off the gray lines, and die almost at once, as on the kalimba. Blown, the stems sit at 1×, 2×, 3×, 4×, …, every one on a line. Each stem’s height is how strong that frequency is in the sound. Same reed; only the way it is played differs.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
How it works
The same bar as a kalimba tine. A reed is riveted at one end and free at the other, so everything worked out on the kalimba page applies unchanged: its modes sit at 1, 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest. Low reeds are long, high reeds are short. The reed’s width does not change its pitch, only how much air it moves.



PreciselyThe reed’s operator and its lowest frequency uses partial derivatives

A reed is riveted at one end and free at the other, so the equation, operator and end conditions of the kalimba page apply unchanged: 
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx}, \qquad u = u_x = 0 \text{ at the rivet}, \qquad u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \text{ at the tip}.
 The mode frequencies are in the ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55. For a rectangular reed of width w and thickness h, I = wh^3/12 and the cross-section area is S = wh, so \kappa^2 = EI/(\rho S) = Eh^2/(12\rho). With \beta_1 = 1.8751/L and \omega = \kappa\beta^2 from the kalimba page, the lowest frequency f_1 = \omega_1/2\pi is 
f_1 = \frac{(1.8751)^2}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{h}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{12\rho}} .
 The width w cancels, so it affects how much air the reed moves, not its pitch.


Blowing turns the reed into a valve. Blow, and the reed swings through its slot, opening and closing the air path hundreds of times a second. The sound comes mainly from the chopped airflow; the acoustics writer Colin Pykett notes that very little comes from the reed’s own motion. A steadily blown reed settles into a motion that repeats itself exactly, at a playing frequency slightly below its first mode’s, so the puffs of air repeat at that rate too. A sound that repeats has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of its repetition rate (page 0). So the blown note lands on the lines, with strong odd and even multiples (Pykett), even though the reed’s own overtones do not. Why the reed locks into one repeating motion is observed, and reproduced by computer models of reeds, but not derived here; the fold gives a plausible picture.



PreciselyWhy a steady train of puffs has only whole-number partials uses Fourier series (page 3)

Let q(t) be the airflow through the slot. Once the blown reed has settled into its steady oscillation, the opening, and so q, repeats every P = 1/f_p seconds: q(t + P) = q(t). A steady oscillation kept going by a steady push, like this one, is called a self-sustained oscillation, and the repeating cycle it settles into a limit cycle; the bowed string and the clarinet reed are others. That it settles into one is observed, and reproduced by nonlinear models of reeds; it is not derived here. A plausible picture, not a derivation: the airflow feeds energy mainly into the first mode, the other modes are not kept going at their own frequencies, and in the repeating cycle they move only as they are pushed, at whole-number multiples of f_p. By the circle page, a periodic function of period P is a Fourier series in \cos(2\pi nt/P) and \sin(2\pi nt/P), so it contains only the frequencies n f_p. How strong each one is depends on the shape of a single puff: short, sharp puffs give strong high partials. The argument uses only that the motion repeats, not which modes make it up, which is why the reed’s own overtone frequencies, 6.27 and 17.55 times f_1, do not appear.
The demo’s sound is a model: one puff shape, chosen so that the open part of each cycle is short, repeated at the playing frequency, then passed through two broad peaks, a stand-in for resonances of the player’s mouth and the instrument. The peaks were set by ear, not measured, so the timbre is approximate. The pitch and the whole-number spacing are not approximations.


The same mechanism drives the bowed string and the clarinet: a steady push, from the bow or the breath, turned into a sound that repeats. On those instruments the string’s or tube’s own frequencies already sit nearly on the lines, so the push and the instrument agree, and locking is easy. A free reed’s own overtones are far off the lines, which lets you hear that the way it is driven, not the reed’s own frequencies, decides where a blown note’s overtones sit.
Tuning a reed with a file. Reed makers tune by scraping metal off, and where they scrape decides the direction. The first mode bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thin the reed near the rivet and you remove stiffness where it counts: the pitch drops. Thin it near the tip and you remove mass where it counts: the pitch rises. It is the spring of page 1 again, where frequency grows with stiffness and falls with mass. Try it below.


    Where to filebase
    
    Blow the filed reedBlow the original
    Filing removes a quarter of the thickness over about a tenth of the reed. The pitch change is estimated as in the fold below.
  




Step-by-step derivationWhy filing moves the pitch: stiffness against mass uses integration by parts and a first-order approximation

The Rayleigh quotient explains the direction. For the first mode, 
\omega_1^2 = \min_{u} \frac{\int_0^L EI\,(u'')^2\,dx}{\int_0^L \rho S\,u^2\,dx},
 the minimum taken over shapes, not identically zero, that satisfy the conditions at the rivet; the minimizing shape is the first mode itself. This is \omega^2 = k/m from page 1 again: stiffness on top, weighted by where the reed bends, and mass at the bottom, weighted by where it moves. The first mode bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thinning the reed near the rivet removes stiffness where it counts and lowers the pitch; thinning it near the tip removes mass where it counts and raises it. The steps below make this quantitative.

The quotient. Multiply \rho S\,\omega^2X = (EI\,X'')'' by X and integrate by parts twice; the boundary terms vanish at the rivet and at the free tip, as on the kalimba page. This gives \omega^2 = \int EI(X'')^2 / \int \rho S X^2 for every mode.
Small change. File the reed so that its thickness changes by \delta h(x) < 0. Then I \propto h^3 changes by \delta(EI) = 3EI\,\delta h/h, and S \propto h changes by \delta(\rho S) = \rho S\,\delta h/h, to first order, that is, ignoring terms in (\delta h)^2.
First order. Because the first mode minimizes the quotient, changing the shape slightly changes the quotient only by an amount proportional to the square of the change. So to first order one may keep the old mode shape X and change only the coefficients: 
\delta(\omega^2) = \frac{\int \frac{\delta h}{h}\,\big(3EI\,(X'')^2 - \omega^2\rho S\,X^2\big)\,dx}{\int \rho S\,X^2\,dx}.

Sign. Near the rivet X \approx 0 and X'' is largest, so the bracket is positive and, with \delta h < 0, \omega drops. Near the tip X'' = 0 and X is largest, so the bracket is negative and \omega rises. In between there is a point where filing changes nothing, to first order.

The demo uses the full quotient with the original mode shape, which is accurate to first order in the depth of filing.


The chromatic slide. A chromatic harmonica has two sets of reed chambers, the second tuned a semitone higher. Each hole has a blow reed, sounded by breathing out, and a draw reed, sounded by breathing in, in each set. Pushing the slide moves a perforated bar that closes one set and opens the other, so every note rises a semitone. In solo tuning, the usual layout for a chromatic harmonica, each group of four holes holds C, E, G, C on the blow and D, F, A, B on the draw. Here is a whole one to play.

    Press and hold a hole. Slide across holes to move between notes.

title: Where did the harmonica reed’s overtones go?
text:
What we found
On the pitch ruler, the plucked reed’s overtones are off the lines and die fast, like a kalimba’s. Blown, the sound repeats, so every frequency in it sits on a line, and you hear a clean note. The operator decides which frequencies an object can vibrate at; the way it is driven decides what you hear.

Same operator as the kalimba. Accordion, concertina and harmonium reeds are free reeds too: they swing freely through a slot, unlike a clarinet’s reed, which beats against the mouthpiece. All of them are cantilevers like the kalimba’s tine: same operator, same ends, smaller and thinner, usually of brass in harmonicas and harmoniums and of steel in accordions and concertinas. What separates a harmonica from a kalimba is the excitation, steady airflow instead of one pluck.

title: Did instruments shape our scales?
text:
← 9 Drum shape · The Shape of a Sound · Map
Pick a sound, then slide the interval between two notes of that sound and listen. The curve shows how rough each interval sounds.

title: Did instruments shape our scales?
text:
On the roughness curve
The curve shows how rough two notes of the chosen sound are, against the ratio between their frequencies, from 1 (the same note) to 3. The dips are the smoothest intervals. With the string-like sound, up to the octave, the dips sit at 6 : 5, 5 : 4, 4 : 3, 3 : 2, 5 : 3 and 2 : 1: the intervals of Western harmony. Switch to the metal bar and the dips move. The octave, 2 : 1, is no longer a dip; a slightly narrower interval, about 1.96, is smoother.

title: Did instruments shape our scales?
text:
How it works
Close partials beat. Two pure tones close in frequency produce beats: their sum swells and fades at the difference of their frequencies. Slow beats sound like a wobble, faster ones like roughness, and once the tones are far enough apart the roughness fades away and you hear two separate, smooth tones. In 1965 Reinier Plomp and Willem Levelt asked listeners how dissonant pairs of pure tones sounded, as a function of their separation; for two pure tones, the answers tracked this roughness. In Sethares’ fit to their results, the roughest separation near middle C is about 22 Hz. A note from a real instrument is several pure tones at once, its partials, so for two notes Sethares adds up the roughness of every pair of partials. That sum is the curve in the demo.



PreciselyThe roughness of two notes, in symbols uses the exponential function

Sethares’ fit to Plomp and Levelt’s data, for two pure tones of equal loudness, the lower at frequency f and the other x hertz above it, is 
\delta(f, x) = e^{-3.5\,s\,x} - e^{-5.75\,s\,x}, \qquad s = \frac{0.24}{0.021\,f + 19},
 with frequencies in hertz. It is zero at x = 0, rises to a peak at x = \ln(5.75/3.5)/(2.25\,s), about 22 Hz near middle C, and then decays. For tones of amplitudes a_1 and a_2, Sethares multiplies by a_1 a_2, as in D(\alpha) below. The factor s makes the roughest separation grow with the frequency, as Plomp and Levelt found: tones high up must be further apart, in hertz, to sound equally smooth. The formula describes average listeners’ judgments of roughness for pure tones; it is a fitted curve, not derived from first principles.
For two notes, Sethares adds up the roughness of every pair of partials, from either note, each weighted by the product of the two partials’ amplitudes: 
D(\alpha) = \sum_{\text{pairs } i < j} a_i a_j\; \delta\big(\min(f_i, f_j),\ |f_i - f_j|\big).
 Here the list f_1, f_2, \dots holds the partials of both notes: those of the lower note, and those of the upper note, whose frequencies are \alpha times the lower note’s; a_i is the amplitude of partial f_i. The roughness \delta of two pure tones depends on how far apart they are and, a little, on how high they are, hence its two inputs. The curve in the demo is D(\alpha). In the demo, the string-like sound has six partials with strengths falling by a factor 0.88 each, and the metal bar has the first four modes of a uniform bar free at both ends, with strengths 1, 0.7, 0.5 and 0.35. Both sets of strengths are chosen for illustration.


Partials that coincide don’t beat. In a string-like sound the partials of the lower note sit at 1, 2, 3, … times its frequency, and those of the upper note at the same multiples of the upper note’s frequency. When the ratio between the notes is a ratio of small whole numbers, say 3 : 2, many partials of the two notes land exactly on each other: the lower note’s third partial and the upper note’s second both sit at three times the lower note’s frequency. Partials that coincide do not beat. Move off 3 : 2 and those pairs pull apart, by a few hertz and then by tens of hertz, into the range where beating sounds roughest. So each simple ratio sits at the bottom of a dip. This extends the idea behind the whole series: frequencies on the lines give a clear pitch, and they also make whole-number intervals smooth.
A metal bar moves the dips. A uniform bar free at both ends, such as a glockenspiel bar, has the kalimba’s operator with different ends, and its partials are at 1, 2.756, 5.404 and 8.933 times the lowest: off the lines. Now the coincidences happen elsewhere. At a ratio of 2.756, the upper note’s lowest partial lands on the lower note’s second. At about 1.961, the upper note’s second partial lands on the lower note’s third (1.961 × 2.756 ≈ 5.404), and that is the dip just below the octave. At exactly 2, nothing lines up. (Xylophone and marimba bars are thinned underneath, in the middle, to move the first overtone onto a whole-number multiple, 3 on a xylophone and 4 on a marimba; gamelan bars are shaped too.)



Step-by-step derivationThe modes of a bar free at both ends uses a 2×2 determinant and hyperbolic functions

The operator is the bar’s \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4 from the kalimba page. A free end carries no bending moment and no shear force, so at both x = 0 and x = L the conditions are X'' = 0 and X''' = 0.

As on the kalimba page, write X = A_1\cos\beta x + A_2\sin\beta x + A_3\cosh\beta x + A_4\sinh\beta x.
At x = 0: X''(0) = \beta^2(-A_1 + A_3) = 0 and X'''(0) = \beta^3(-A_2 + A_4) = 0, so A_3 = A_1 and A_4 = A_2. Then X = A_1(\cos\beta x + \cosh\beta x) + A_2(\sin\beta x + \sinh\beta x).
At x = L, dividing by \beta^2 and \beta^3 and writing C_1 = \cos\beta L, S_1 = \sin\beta L, C_2 = \cosh\beta L, S_2 = \sinh\beta L, as on the kalimba page: 
(C_2 - C_1)\,A_1 + (S_2 - S_1)\,A_2 = 0, \qquad (S_2 + S_1)\,A_1 + (C_2 - C_1)\,A_2 = 0 .

These have a solution other than A_1 = A_2 = 0 exactly when the determinant is zero: (C_2 - C_1)^2 - (S_2 - S_1)(S_2 + S_1) = (C_2^2 - S_2^2) + (C_1^2 + S_1^2) - 2C_1C_2 = 2 - 2C_1C_2, using C_2^2 - S_2^2 = 1 and C_1^2 + S_1^2 = 1. So 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1 .
 Besides \beta = 0, which belongs to the bar moving or rotating rigidly without bending, the roots are \beta L = 4.7300,\ 7.8532,\ 10.9956,\ 14.1372, \dots, computed on this page. Since the frequency is proportional to \beta^2, the partials are at (\beta_n/\beta_1)^2 = 1,\ 2.756,\ 5.404,\ 8.933 times the lowest.



The gamelan. Sethares measured the spectra of gamelan metallophones, instruments of tuned metal bars, and reports that “the dissonance curve for these metallophones have minima that occur at or near the scale steps used by the gamelans”. The demo’s bars are idealized, not measured gamelan bars, so it shows the mechanism, not his result; real gamelan bars are shaped by their makers, and tunings vary from one gamelan to another.
Roughness is not the whole story. The curve measures sensory roughness, which is one ingredient of what sounds pleasant, not all of it. In a study of more than 250 American college students, Josh McDermott, Andriana Lehr and Andrew Oxenham found in 2010 that liking for consonant chords followed harmonicity, whether the frequencies fit one harmonic series, more than it followed beating, and grew with musical training. In 2016 McDermott and colleagues found that the Tsimane’, a society in the Bolivian Amazon with little exposure to Western music, rated consonant and dissonant chords as equally pleasant, although they disliked roughness just as other groups did.

title: Did instruments shape our scales?
text:
What we found
An instrument’s spectrum does not only decide whether it has a pitch. It decides which pairs of notes sound smooth together on it: for instruments with their partials on the lines, the simple whole-number ratios of Western harmony; for metal bars, with their partials off the lines, other intervals. That much is a fact about sound and the ear. What a culture finds beautiful is also learned. Sethares argues that instruments and the scales played on them tend to fit each other in the way the demo shows; how much that shaped the world’s music is an open, argued question.

text:
On the pitch ruler

Higher up the stems crowd together, so some land near a line by chance, such as 2.92× and 4.06×; but no base frequency in the range we hear as pitch puts them all on or near lines. Each stem’s height is how strongly that mode sounds at the listening ring for the strike you made: strike somewhere else and the heights change, never the positions. Tap a stem to see that mode on the drumhead and hear it alone.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
How it works
A sheet pulled tight. On a string, tension pulls each point toward the average height of its two neighbors. On a sheet, it pulls each point toward the average height of all the points around it, and the further a point sits from that average, the harder it is pulled back. The rim is held still. In the series’ language, this rule, written with the Laplacian, is the drum’s operator, and the still rim is its boundary condition.



Step-by-step derivationThe drum’s equation, from Newton’s law for a patch uses partial derivatives and the divergence theorem

The operator. A drumhead with tension T, measured as force per unit length of any cut through it, and mass \sigma per unit area obeys 
u_{tt} = c^2\,\Delta u, \qquad \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\sigma}, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on the rim}.
 The operator is -c^2\Delta; \Delta, the Laplacian, adds the second partial derivatives in the two directions across the sheet. On a string, the restoring force was proportional to how far a point sits below the average of its two neighbors; on a sheet it is proportional to how far a point sits below the average of the points around it, and that is what \Delta u measures.


    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      patch DT ds
    
    Tension pulls outward all around the edge. Where the sheet bulges, the pulls tilt and their vertical parts add up to T times the Laplacian of u, per unit area.
  


Take any small patch D of the head. Along each short piece ds of its edge, the sheet outside pulls with force T\,ds, along the surface and outward.
For small slopes the vertical part of that pull is T\,\partial_n u\,ds, where \partial_n u is the slope of the head in the outward direction across the edge. This is the string’s T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta again.
Add these up around the edge. The divergence theorem turns the sum around the edge into a sum over the inside: 
T\oint_{\partial D} \partial_n u\,ds = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA .

Newton’s law for the patch reads \iint_D \sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA. This holds for every patch, however small, so the integrands are equal at every point: \sigma u_{tt} = T\Delta u.

In one dimension a patch is a segment, its edge is its two endpoints, and step 3 is the fundamental theorem of calculus, u_x(b) - u_x(a) = \int_a^b u_{xx}\,dx. That is the string’s equation again.
What was assumed: small slopes, a tension that is the same everywhere and does not change as the head moves, no bending stiffness, and no air. The air matters for real drums, as the timpani section below says.


Spokes and circles. On a round drum, each mode has its own pattern of still lines: some straight lines through the center, like spokes, and some circles around it. Going once around the drum, a mode must come back to itself, so around the center it repeats a whole number of times: the loop of page 3, inside the drum. Outward from the center, the shape is a Bessel function, a wave whose swings slowly shrink, and the rim must sit exactly where that wave crosses zero.
Why the frequencies miss the lines. Those zero crossings set the frequencies. For the modes with no spokes, the crossings come at nearly even steps, but the first step is short, so the later crossings are not multiples of the first: the frequencies go 1 : 2.30 : 3.60. Each number of spokes gives its own sequence, shifted by a different amount, and the sequences interleave at unrelated places. Merged, they give the drum’s list 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, 2.65×, 2.92×, …, scattered between the lines. One more pattern: every mode with spokes comes in a pair, the same pattern turned, with exactly the same frequency. That is the round drum’s symmetry, heard in its spectrum.



PreciselyBessel functions and the frequencies of a round drum uses polar coordinates

A mode is a fixed shape X swinging as X\cos\omega t, with -\Delta X = k^2 X where k = \omega/c, and X = 0 on the rim. For a round drum of radius a, measure position by the distance r from the center and the angle \theta. Going once around the drum, a mode must return to itself, so its dependence on the angle is \cos m\theta or \sin m\theta with m a whole number, and its dependence on r is a Bessel function, so the modes are 
J_m(k r)\cos m\theta \quad\text{and}\quad J_m(kr)\sin m\theta, \qquad m = 0, 1, 2, \dots
 The Bessel function J_m plays the part that the sine played on a string: it wiggles like a cosine or sine whose swings slowly shrink. Its zeros are not whole-number multiples of the first one: those of J_0 are at 2.405,\ 5.520,\ 8.654, \dots, in the ratios 1 : 2.30 : 3.60. They are spaced by about \pi, but shifted: the first is about 0.77\pi, not \pi, so the later ones are not multiples of it. J_0 starts at 1 at the center; J_1, J_2, … start at 0.











J₀ (starts at 1)J₁ (starts at 0)

The rim condition J_m(ka) = 0 says ka must be a zero of J_m. Writing j_{m,n} for the n-th positive zero, k = j_{m,n}/a and f = ck/2\pi, so 
f_{m,n} = \frac{c\,j_{m,n}}{2\pi a}.
 Listed in order, the frequencies relative to the lowest are 1,\ 1.593,\ 2.136,\ 2.295,\ 2.653,\ 2.917, \dots No base frequency in the pitch range puts them near whole-number multiples: the zeros of each J_m are spaced by about \pi but shifted, by an amount that depends on m, and the zeros of J_0, of J_1, of J_2 and so on interleave at unrelated places. So the sound does not repeat and there is no clear pitch. Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to two modes, the cosine and the sine, which are the same pattern turned: the round head’s symmetry, visible as a multiplicity of 2.





Step-by-step derivationSeparation of variables in polar coordinates uses partial derivatives


Look for a fixed shape. A mode is u = X(r, \theta)\cos\omega t with -\Delta X = k^2X, k = \omega/c, and X = 0 at r = a.
Laplacian in polar coordinates. \Delta X = X_{rr} + \frac1r X_r + \frac{1}{r^2}X_{\theta\theta}.
Separate. Try X = R(r)\,\Theta(\theta), a separation of variables. Substituting and multiplying by r^2/(R\Theta) gives 
\frac{r^2R'' + rR' + k^2r^2R}{R} = -\frac{\Theta''}{\Theta}.
 The left side depends only on r, the right only on \theta, so both equal one constant.
The angle. Going once around the drum must return \Theta to itself, so -\Theta'' = m^2\Theta with \Theta periodic. This is exactly the eigenvalue problem of the circle page: m is a whole number and \Theta = \cos m\theta or \sin m\theta.
The radius. What remains is Bessel’s equation, r^2R'' + rR' + (k^2r^2 - m^2)R = 0. It has two independent solutions; one, J_m(kr), is finite at the center, and the other becomes infinite there. For m = 0 that would correspond to a point force pushing on the center of the head, and for m \ge 1 to something even more singular; in every case its energy is infinite, so it is not a free mode.
The rim. R(a) = 0 means J_m(ka) = 0, so ka must be one of the zeros j_{m,1} < j_{m,2} < \cdots of J_m.

Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to exactly two modes because Bessel functions of different whole-number orders never share a positive zero; this was conjectured by Bourget and proved by Carl Ludwig Siegel in 1929. The zeros have no closed form; this page computes them numerically. For large n they approach j_{m,n} \approx (n + \tfrac m2 - \tfrac14)\pi, evenly spaced for one fixed m, but the different m interleave, and the low ones are not close to any common grid.


The sand draws the still lines. In 1808 Ernst Chladni showed the French Institute in Paris, the body that then held the Academy of Sciences, a trick: sprinkle sand on a metal plate, draw a violin bow along its edge, and the sand leaps into a pattern, a different one for each note. The sand is jostled wherever the plate moves and comes to rest where it doesn’t, so each pattern is one mode’s still lines. Here is the same trick on a drumhead: pick a frequency and watch where the sand goes.


  
  
  Sprinkle fresh sandHear this note
  
  Each button drives the drumhead at one of its own frequencies, given as a multiple of the lowest. Every grain is jostled in proportion to how much the head moves under it, so grains drift until they reach a place where the head stays still. Chladni used stiff metal plates, whose operator involves bending, not tension; the sand behaves the same way on both.


Napoleon offered a prize for explaining the patterns. Sophie Germain won it in 1816, the first woman to receive the Paris Academy’s grand prize in mathematics, with a theory that still had errors; Gustav Kirchhoff gave the full theory of vibrating plates, with the correct edge conditions, in 1850. Finding the still lines and finding the frequencies are one problem: on a drumhead, the one on this page; on a plate, the same problem with the plate’s own operator.



PreciselyWhere the sand collects uses polar coordinates

The mode J_m(kr)\cos m\theta with k = j_{m,n}/a is zero where \cos m\theta = 0, at 2m angles, which pair up into m lines through the center, and along the circles where J_m(kr) = 0 inside the rim, n - 1 of them for the n-th zero. Those are exactly the lines where the sand collects.


Where you strike. A sharp strike starts each mode in proportion to how far that mode moves at the point struck. Every mode with spokes stays still at the center, so a strike at dead center sounds only the round modes, those with no spokes; a strike on one of a mode’s still lines leaves that mode silent. Timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out from the center, near the still lines of several modes, which keeps those modes quiet (HyperPhysics).



DetailsHow strongly a strike excites each mode, in this model uses integrals over an area

Number the modes X_1, X_2, \dots in order of frequency. A sharp strike, a brief push at a point p, gives mode i a starting speed in proportion to X_i(p), the mode’s height at the point struck, the same rule as the piano’s hammer on page 7. We model what you hear as the speed of the head at a listening point q, which picks up mode i in proportion to X_i(q). Dividing by \iint X_i^2\,dA, the integral of the mode’s square over the head, removes the arbitrary size of each shape. So mode i sounds with weight X_i(p)\,X_i(q)\big/\iint X_i^2\,dA. (A real drum radiates sound from its whole head, and some modes radiate better than others; this model ignores that.) For the timpani strike point: for the first four modes with one still circle inside, that circle lies between 0.44 and 0.65 of the radius. The lowest mode, which dies away fast and is not musically useful, is excited less there than by a strike at the center.


The exception: timpani. A timpani does have a pitch. Its kettle and the air it encloses shift the head’s modes enough to matter: measured, the modes with one, two, three and four lines through the center, and no still circle inside, sit close to 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a common base frequency (HyperPhysics; Fletcher and Rossing). The note is normally heard at the first of these, the “2”, with the next two a fifth and an octave above it (Vienna’s Institute of Musical Acoustics); the missing base, an octave lower, may be heard instead (HyperPhysics). Pulled near the lines, the drum gives a note.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
What we found
On the pitch ruler, a drum’s frequencies are off the lines, and its sound fades fast: a thud. The drum taught three things. A round drum’s modes come in families, one for each number of spokes. Within a family the steps between frequencies are nearly even but the first step is short, and the families interleave, so the frequencies miss the lines. And the drum’s round symmetry shows up as pairs of modes with exactly the same frequency. Change what surrounds the head, as a timpani’s kettle does, and the frequencies can be pulled back near the lines.

Same operator, different constants, as a first model. Toms, snares and timpani share this operator on a disk. They differ in tension, size and the mass of the head, and in what surrounds it, and the air in and around a drum changes the operator a little.

title: Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?
text:
How it works
A wave must close up. A loop has no ends: a wave that runs once around must arrive back exactly where it started. So the simple waves on a loop have a whole number of crests, 1, 2, 3, …, plus one motion with none, in which the whole loop lifts at once and makes no sound. As the beads crowd together, the bead equation of page 2 becomes the equation of a continuous string, the wave equation.



Step-by-step derivationFrom beads to the wave equation uses partial derivatives and Taylor’s theorem

Measure position around the loop by the angle \theta, and choose units so that the loop has circumference 2\pi. Bead j sits at \theta_j = jh with h = 2\pi/N. Let \mu be the mass per unit length, so each bead has mass m = \mu h, and write u(\theta, t) for the height of the loop at angle \theta and time t, so that u_j(t) = u(\theta_j, t). On a string of tension T, bead j feels the force \frac{T}{h}(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}) (page 2). Dividing by m gives 
\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{\mu}\cdot\frac{u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}}{h^2}.
 The fraction on the right has a simple meaning. (u_{j+1} - u_j)/h is the slope of the string just to the right of bead j, and (u_j - u_{j-1})/h the slope just to the left. Their difference, divided by h once more, measures how fast the slope changes: the second derivative. So as the beads crowd together, h \to 0, the bead equation becomes 
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2\,\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial \theta^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}.
 Here u depends on two things, the angle and the time. The symbol \partial u/\partial t, a partial derivative, is the derivative in time with the angle held fixed, and \partial u/\partial\theta the derivative in angle with the time held fixed; the second derivatives are also written u_{tt} and u_{\theta\theta}. This is the wave equation. The constant c is the speed at which a bump travels around the loop; the second demo below shows it.
Why the second difference becomes the second derivative. Expand the neighbors with Taylor’s theorem, assuming the shape has four continuous derivatives: 
u(\theta \pm h) = u \pm h\,u' + \tfrac{h^2}{2}u'' \pm \tfrac{h^3}{6}u''' + O(h^4),
 where O(h^4) stands for terms no bigger than a constant times h^4. Add the two expansions and subtract 2u. The odd terms cancel in pairs: 
u(\theta + h) - 2u(\theta) + u(\theta - h) = h^2 u''(\theta) + O(h^4).
 Divide by h^2: the fraction equals u'' + O(h^2), which tends to u''. (For the table above: on a ring of N beads, mode k’s frequency divided by mode 1’s is \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N), from page 2, which tends to k as N grows.) What was held fixed: the circumference, the tension T, and the mass per length \mu. So as the beads multiply, each one gets lighter in proportion.

  
  
  
  
  θ − hθθ + h
  gap ≈ −h² u''/2

The middle bead sits above the average of its neighbors by about -\tfrac{h^2}{2}u'', which is positive where the curve bends down (u'' < 0). That is why the force on a bead, and so its acceleration, is proportional to the curvature u''.


A shorter wave is pulled back harder. On a string, the pull on each bit is proportional to how sharply the string bends there. Squeeze a wave into half the length, at the same height, and it bends 4 times as sharply (the slope doubles, and it changes over half the distance: 2 × 2 = 4), so the pull is 4 times as strong. A wave with n crests is n times shorter than the one-crest wave, so it is pulled back n² times harder. Frequency goes as the square root of the pull, as for the mass on a spring (page 1), so the wave with n crests swings exactly n times faster than the one-crest wave.



Step-by-step derivationThe operator, its eigenfunctions and the frequencies uses derivatives

The operator. Write the wave equation as 
u_{tt} = -c^2 A u, \qquad A = -\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}.
 The operator A takes a shape f(\theta) and returns a new shape, -f''. Strictly, the operator in the sense of the series page, minus the restoring force per unit mass, is c^2A; the constant c^2 only scales the eigenvalues, so this page works with A and puts c back in the frequencies. The minus sign is a convention that makes A of a bump positive at the bump; the restoring force per unit mass is -c^2 Af, which pulls the bump back down. If you read page 2, A is the continuous version of the beads’ matrix K/h^2.
Which shapes. A shape on the loop is a function f(\theta) that returns to itself after one turn: f(\theta + 2\pi) = f(\theta).
Eigenfunctions and eigenvalues. An eigenfunction of A is a shape that A only rescales: Af = \lambda f for some number \lambda, called the eigenvalue. Try \cos n\theta, a wave with n crests around the loop. Its second derivative is -n^2\cos n\theta, so 
A\cos n\theta = n^2\cos n\theta, \qquad A\sin n\theta = n^2\sin n\theta .
 These shapes close up after one turn exactly when n is a whole number. So the spectrum of A, the list of its eigenvalues, is 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, \dots Each n^2 with n \ge 1 belongs to two eigenfunctions, \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta, which are the same wave shifted by a quarter of a wavelength; n = 0 belongs to the constant shape, the whole loop lifted at once. The proof fold a little further down shows that there are no other eigenvalues.
Frequencies. The shape \cos(n\theta)\cos(\omega t) solves the wave equation when \omega^2 = c^2 n^2: differentiate it twice in t and twice in \theta and compare. Here \omega is the angular frequency, in radians per second, and the frequency in hertz is f = \omega/2\pi. So mode n sounds at f_n = cn/2\pi, exactly n times the lowest. (In ordinary units, for a loop of circumference \ell, this is f_n = nc/\ell: the time for a bump to travel once around, \ell/c, is the period of the lowest mode.) The eigenvalues are perfect squares; the frequencies, proportional to their square roots, are whole-number multiples of one frequency. The table under the first demo shows the ring of beads approaching this from below.





Reader questionHow is a mode’s shape related to its swinging in time?

Both come from separating variables. Look for a motion in which the shape stays fixed and only its size changes: u = X(\theta)\,q(t). Substituting into u_{tt} = c^2u_{\theta\theta} and dividing by Xq gives q''/q = c^2X''/X. The left side depends only on t and the right only on \theta. Changing t alone cannot change the right side, so the left side cannot change either; the same holds the other way round, so both sides equal one constant. That constant cannot be positive, because A has no negative eigenvalues (Step 1 of the proof below), so we call it -\omega^2. That splits the equation in two. In time, q'' = -\omega^2 q, so q = \cos(\omega t + \phi), times any constant: the mass on a spring. (For \omega = 0 the solution is q = a + bt instead: the loop drifts as a whole.) In space, -X'' = (\omega/c)^2 X with X periodic: the eigenvalue problem for A, which allows only \omega/c = n. The space part chooses the frequency, and the time part swings at it. The time factor is a cosine, for every nonzero frequency, for every instrument in this series, because every operator here has no negative eigenvalues and every equation has two time derivatives and no friction term; damping, added on page 7, multiplies the cosine by a decaying factor. Everything instrument-specific lives in the space part.


In the series’ language, the rule that takes a shape and returns the pull on it is the loop’s operator. The waves with n crests are the shapes it only rescales, its eigenfunctions. The scale factors, proportional to 0, 1, 4, 9, …, are its eigenvalues, and their list is its spectrum. The frequencies go as their square roots: 0, 1, 2, 3, … times one base frequency. This loop is the smallest example in the series of an operator and its spectrum.



ProofThe eigenvalues are exactly 0, 1, 4, 9, … uses integration by parts

Step 1: no eigenvalue is negative. For periodic shapes f and g, integrate by parts twice. The boundary terms are values at \theta = 2\pi minus values at \theta = 0, which cancel because the shapes are periodic: 
\int_0^{2\pi} (Af)\,g\,d\theta = -\int_0^{2\pi} f''g\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} f'g'\,d\theta = -\int_0^{2\pi} f g''\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,(Ag)\,d\theta .
 An operator with this property is called symmetric, by analogy with a symmetric matrix. (With the right choice of allowed shapes it is also self-adjoint, the stronger property that the spectral theorem in the complex-numbers fold further down needs.) If Af = \lambda f with f not identically zero, take g = f in the middle expression: \lambda\int_0^{2\pi} f^2\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}(f')^2\,d\theta \ge 0, so \lambda \ge 0. (For a complex-valued f, use \int f\bar f\,d\theta = \int |f|^2\,d\theta instead, as in the complex-numbers fold further down; the same computation shows that \lambda is real and at least 0.)
Step 2: solve the equation. Af = \lambda f means f'' = -\lambda f.

If \lambda = 0, then f = a + b\theta, which returns to itself after one turn only when b = 0. Eigenvalue 0, eigenfunctions the constants.
If \lambda > 0, write \lambda = s^2 with s > 0; then f = a\cos s\theta + b\sin s\theta, a wave that repeats every 2\pi/s radians. It returns to itself after one full turn exactly when 2\pi is a whole number of these periods, that is, when s is a whole number n. Eigenvalue n^2, eigenfunctions \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta.

Step 3: eigenfunctions for different eigenvalues are perpendicular, in the sense used below: \int_0^{2\pi} \cos n\theta\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0 for n \ne m, and similarly for sines and for a sine against a cosine. This can be checked directly with the product formulas for cosines, and it also follows from Step 1, just as for a symmetric matrix.
For readers who know functional analysis: A is not defined on every square-integrable function, only on those with two derivatives in L^2, the Sobolev space H^2(S^1). On that domain it is self-adjoint, not merely symmetric: in Fourier coefficients it is multiplication by n^2 on the sequences with \sum n^4|c_n|^2 < \infty. That there is no spectrum besides these eigenvalues follows from the completeness of the eigenfunctions, proved in the complex-numbers fold further down.





Reader questionThe equation of one wave has one frequency in it. Where does an infinite list come from?

In the equation u'' + k^2u = 0, the number k is chosen in advance, and for each k it has the two solutions \cos k\theta and \sin k\theta. The eigenvalue question runs the other way: for which k does a solution go once around the loop and come back to itself? Every whole number k does, and nothing limits how many times a wave may wind around, so the list never ends. The count matches the number of ways the system can move: N beads have N eigenvalues, counted with repetitions, and a continuous loop has infinitely many.
For readers who know functional analysis: on an infinite straight string, with no loop to close up and no ends, every k \ge 0 gives a bounded wave e^{ikx} and the spectrum is the whole half-line [0, \infty). Strictly, these waves are not eigenfunctions, because \int|e^{ikx}|^2\,dx is infinite. This is one reason the general definition of spectrum is more than a list of eigenvalues. A bounded instrument, closed up or with ends that are not too irregular, has a discrete list.


Why beads fall short. A bead feels only its two neighbors. When a crest is many beads wide, that is enough to sense the bend almost exactly. When a crest is only a few beads wide, the neighbors sit partway down the wave, and the bead underestimates how sharply the string bends. So the pull is weaker than n² times, and the frequency falls short of n×, the more so the shorter the wave. Crowd in more beads and any given wave becomes many beads wide: its shortfall vanishes.
Every shape is a sum of these waves. From the 1740s on, Jean d’Alembert, Leonhard Euler and Daniel Bernoulli argued about the vibrating string. D’Alembert showed in 1747 that a string can move in essentially any smooth shape. Bernoulli held that every vibration is a sum of simple modes, which for a string are sine-shaped. Euler, who allowed a plucked string’s sharp corner as a starting shape, objected that a sum of sines could not represent such arbitrary shapes, and d’Alembert doubted that such a sum was physical at all.
Bernoulli was right, in a sense that took mathematicians more than a century to make precise. Every shape of the loop, corners included, is a sum of its simple waves: its Fourier series. The doubt is natural, since every wave is smooth and a corner is not, but an infinite sum of smooth waves need not be smooth. Released, each wave swings at its own frequency, and all of them are whole-number multiples of the lowest, so the whole motion repeats, and any sound it makes has a pitch. Build a plucked shape out of waves, then let it go:


  
  Waves used, up to
  Let goHear the loop, at the plucked point
  
  The loop is cut open and laid flat; its two edges are the same point. Dashed: the exact motion (once let go, the bump splits into two half-height copies that travel apart). Solid: the sum of the waves so far, each swinging at its own frequency.





Step-by-step derivationHow much of each wave a shape contains uses integrals

The Fourier series is the eigenfunction expansion. With the beads we wrote the starting shape as a sum of eigenvectors and let each one swing on its own. Here the same move reads 
f(\theta) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta\big),
 the Fourier series of f. To find the numbers a_n and b_n, use the fact that the eigenfunctions are perpendicular. For whole numbers n \ne m, 
\int_0^{2\pi}\cos n\theta\,\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0, \qquad \int_0^{2\pi}\sin n\theta\,\sin m\theta\,d\theta = 0,
 while \int_0^{2\pi}\cos n\theta\,\sin m\theta\,d\theta = 0 for all n and m, and \int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 n\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2 n\theta\,d\theta = \pi for n \ge 1. To check them, turn each product into a sum with \cos A\cos B = \tfrac12[\cos(A - B) + \cos(A + B)] and its relatives for sines; every cosine or sine of a nonzero whole-number multiple of \theta integrates to zero over a full turn. These integrals are the continuous version of the dot product: for two columns of bead heights, \sum_j u_j v_j\,h is a dot product times h, and as the beads crowd together it becomes \int f g\,d\theta. Now multiply both sides of the series by \cos m\theta and integrate from 0 to 2\pi. Every term drops out except the one with n = m, which leaves \pi a_m. So 
a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\cos n\theta\,d\theta, \qquad b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\sin n\theta\,d\theta,
 just as a vector’s component along an axis is its dot product with that axis. The constant term is written a_0/2 so that the same formula also gives a_0: for n = 0, \int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 0\,d\theta = 2\pi, not \pi. Released from rest in the shape f, each eigenfunction swings at its own frequency: 
u(\theta, t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta\big)\cos(c\,n\,t).
 Every term returns to its starting value after the time 2\pi/c, so the whole motion repeats. The demo above builds a plucked shape, corner and all, out of cosines and lets it go. The next fold gives the same series in complex notation and states the theorem that settles the old argument.





PreciselyThe same series with complex numbers, and why every shape is a sum of waves uses complex numbers; the second half, functional analysis

With complex numbers. With Euler’s formula e^{in\theta} = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta, the pair \cos n\theta, \sin n\theta can be traded for the pair e^{in\theta}, e^{-in\theta}, and A e^{in\theta} = n^2 e^{in\theta}. The Fourier series becomes 
f(\theta) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n\,e^{in\theta}, \qquad c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\,e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta ,
 with c_{\pm n} = (a_n \mp i b_n)/2 for n \ge 1 and c_0 = a_0/2. The perpendicularity above becomes \langle e^{in\theta}, e^{im\theta}\rangle = 0 for n \ne m, for the inner product \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,\bar g\,d\theta; the bar, complex conjugation, is what makes \langle f, f\rangle a positive number for complex-valued f. The natural space of shapes is L^2(S^1), all functions on the circle S^1 with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta finite: the shapes of finite “total squared height”.
Every shape is a sum of eigenfunctions. The functions e^{in\theta}/\sqrt{2\pi}, n \in \mathbb{Z}, form an orthonormal basis of L^2(S^1). That is, for every f in L^2(S^1), 
\Big\| f - \sum_{|n| \le M} c_n e^{in\theta} \Big\| \to 0 \quad (M \to \infty), \qquad \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta = \sum_n |c_n|^2 ,
 the second identity being Parseval’s.
Why it needs a proof. For a symmetric N\times N matrix, N perpendicular eigenvectors automatically span everything, because the space has dimension N. Here there are infinitely many eigenfunctions and the space is infinite-dimensional, so one has to show that no shape is perpendicular to all of them. One standard proof shows that trigonometric sums can approximate any continuous periodic function uniformly (Fejér’s theorem), and that continuous functions are dense in L^2. See Stein and Shakarchi, chapters 2 and 3.
Pointwise. Convergence in L^2 is convergence of the total squared error. At individual points more care is needed: there are continuous functions whose Fourier series diverge at a point. For the shapes on this page, continuous and made of straight pieces, the series converges at every point. The plucked triangle’s coefficients shrink like 1/n^2, which is why a few terms already look right in the demo.
What it took. The old argument could not be settled until “sum” had a precise meaning for infinitely many terms. Fourier claimed such expansions for arbitrary functions in his 1807 work on heat. Dirichlet proved in 1829 that the series converges at every point for a broad class of functions, including shapes with corners; the L^2 statement above belongs to the early 20th century; and that the Fourier series of every L^2 function converges at almost every point was proved only in 1966, by Lennart Carleson (Wikipedia). In the L^2 sense, Bernoulli was right, and a corner is no obstacle.
The pattern for every later page. Each instrument’s operator A will be self-adjoint and nonnegative, and (A + 1)^{-1} will be a compact operator. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators then gives the same three facts as here: a list of real eigenvalues growing to infinity, perpendicular eigenfunctions, and an expansion of every shape in them. Only the list and the shapes change.

title: Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?
text:
What we found
A wave on a loop must close up, so it has a whole number of crests, and a string pulls a wave n times shorter back n² times harder, so it swings n times faster. That is why the loop’s frequencies land exactly on the lines. In the series’ language, the loop’s operator has eigenvalues 0, 1, 4, 9, …, and writing a shape as a sum of its eigenfunctions is the Fourier series. Every later page has the same pattern with a different operator: a list of eigenvalues that grows without end, and a set of simple shapes from which every shape is built. Only the list and the shapes change.

The Shape of a Sound · Map · Glossary
Technical words in the series link here, usually the first time they appear on a page. Each entry gives a plain definition and a link to a fuller explanation.

title: Glossary
text:
Sound

Hertz (Hz)

One cycle per second, the unit of frequency. The A above middle C is tuned to 440 Hz. Wikipedia

Periodic

A signal p(t) is periodic with period P > 0 if it repeats exactly every P seconds: p(t + P) = p(t) for all t. Its shortest such P is usually what is meant by the period. Wikipedia

Pitch

How high or low a note sounds. For a periodic sound with shortest period P, the pitch is heard at the repetition rate 1/P, even when no component at that frequency is present, as long as that rate is between a few dozen and a few thousand per second. Wikipedia, and page 0

Partial, overtone

A sound can be split into components of single frequencies; each one is a partial. An overtone is any partial above the lowest. Wikipedia

Fundamental

For a periodic sound, the frequency f = 1/P at which it repeats; its harmonics are the whole-number multiples of f. It is usually the lowest and strongest partial, but it can be weak or even missing, and the pitch is still heard at f (page 0). For a sound that is not periodic, such as a drum’s, “fundamental” just means the lowest partial. Wikipedia

Harmonic

A partial at a whole-number multiple nf of the fundamental. A periodic sound contains only harmonics. Wikipedia

Harmonic series

The whole-number multiples f, 2f, 3f, \dots of one frequency f. All the partials of a periodic sound belong to one harmonic series. Wikipedia

Inharmonic

Having partials that are not whole-number multiples of one frequency. A bell, a drum and a kalimba tine are strongly inharmonic; a piano string is slightly inharmonic. Wikipedia

Timbre

What tells two notes of the same pitch and loudness apart, such as a violin and a flute both playing A. It depends mostly on the relative strengths of the partials and how they change over the course of the note. Wikipedia

Note names: C4, A4, middle C

Notes are named by a letter from A to G and an octave number. C4 is middle C, about 262 Hz, near the middle of the piano keyboard; C5 is the C an octave above it; A4 is the A at 440 Hz. Wikipedia

Semitone

The smallest step on a piano, from one key to the next, white or black. Twelve semitones make an octave. Wikipedia

Equal temperament

The usual way of tuning a piano: every semitone is the same frequency ratio, 2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595, so twelve of them make an exact octave. The price is that the other intervals miss the simple ratios slightly: an equal-tempered fifth is 2^{7/12} \approx 1.4983, not 3/2. Wikipedia

Cent

A unit for small differences in pitch: one hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone, so an octave is 1200 cents. Two frequencies in the ratio r are 1200\log_2 r cents apart. Trained listeners notice a few cents. Wikipedia

Octave, fifth, twelfth

Musical intervals, named by frequency ratio. An octave is a ratio of 2. A fifth is the ratio 3/2 when tuned to the simple ratio, and 2^{7/12} \approx 1.498 in equal temperament. A twelfth, an octave plus a fifth, is about 3. Smaller intervals, by their simple ratios: the minor third 6/5, the major third 5/4, the fourth 4/3 and the major sixth 5/3. Two notes an octave apart sound like “the same note, higher”. Wikipedia

Beats

When two pure tones of nearly equal frequency sound together, their sum swells and fades in loudness at a rate equal to the difference of their frequencies. Tuners listen for beats; fast beats are heard as roughness. Wikipedia

Consonance, roughness

Consonance is how smooth or stable two notes sound together. Roughness is one ingredient of it: the harsh quality of fast beats between partials that are close but not equal. Wikipedia, and the epilogue

title: Glossary
text:
Instrument parts and playing

Nut, bridge

On a string instrument, the two points that end a string’s vibrating length: the nut at the top of the neck, the bridge on the body. The bridge also carries the string’s vibration to the body, or on a piano to the soundboard. On a kalimba, the bridge is the bar the tines are pressed against. Wikipedia

Open string

A string played with no finger pressing it down, so its whole length between the nut and the bridge vibrates. Wikipedia

Harmonics, on a string

Notes a string player gets by touching the string lightly at a fraction of its length, such as the middle, instead of pressing it down. Only the modes with a still point under the finger keep sounding. Wikipedia, and page 4

Overblowing, register key

Making a wind instrument’s air column jump to a higher mode. A flutist overblows by blowing faster; a clarinetist presses the register key, which opens a small hole that spoils the lowest mode. Wikipedia, and page 5

Blow, draw

On a harmonica, a blow note sounds when you breathe out through a hole, and a draw note when you breathe in. Each hole has one reed for each (on a chromatic harmonica, one for each in each of its two sets). Wikipedia

Free reed

A thin metal tongue fixed at one end that swings through a closely fitting slot, opening and shutting it like a valve. Harmonicas and accordions use free reeds. Wikipedia

Damper

A felt pad that rests on a piano string and stops it when the key is released. Each key lifts its own damper while held; the right pedal lifts them all. The highest strings, roughly the top 20 keys, have no dampers. Wikipedia: Sustain pedal

Soft pedal, una corda

The left pedal of a piano. On a grand it shifts the hammers sideways so they hit fewer strings; this is the una corda, Italian for “one string”. On an upright it instead moves the hammers closer to the strings, so they strike more gently. Wikipedia

Practice pedal, mute

The middle pedal on many uprights. It lowers a strip of felt between the hammers and the strings, making the sound much quieter and duller. Wikipedia: Piano pedals

title: Glossary
text:
Vibration

Partial derivative, u_t, u_{xx}

For a function of several variables, such as the height u(x, t) of a string at position x and time t, the rate of change in one variable with the others held fixed. Subscripts name the variable: u_t is the velocity of the point at x, u_{tt} its acceleration, u_x the slope of the string, and u_{xx} how fast that slope changes along it, which for small slopes is its curvature. Wikipedia

Proportional, \propto

a \propto b means that a is a fixed number times b. So f \propto 1/L^2 means that halving L multiplies f by four. Wikipedia

Angular frequency

\omega = 2\pi f: the frequency counted in radians per second instead of cycles per second, one cycle being 2\pi radians. Formulas such as \omega^2 = k/m are shortest in \omega. Wikipedia

Wavenumber

The counterpart of angular frequency in space: a wave \sin kx has wavenumber k = 2\pi/\text{wavelength}. For the wave equation, \omega = ck. Wikipedia

Linear

An equation with no outside force is linear if sums and multiples of solutions are again solutions. An equation with an outside force is linear when it reads (left side) = (the force), where the force does not involve u, and the left side is built from u and its derivatives only by multiplying each by a number, or by a given function of position and time, and adding: no u^2, no u\,u_x, no \sin u. The piano page’s \mu u_{tt} + b\,u_t - Tu_{xx} + EI\,u_{xxxx} = f(x, t) is an example. Then the difference of any two solutions solves the same equation without the force. The operators in this series are linear, a good model for the small vibrations of instruments. What keeps a bowed string, a clarinet reed or a harmonica reed going is not linear: the bow’s grip and slip and a reed opening and closing. Wikipedia

Superposition

Adding solutions of a linear equation to get another solution. The free motion of an instrument, once nothing is driving it, is a superposition, a sum, of its modes. Wikipedia

Mode, normal mode

A motion of an object, with no friction and nothing driving it, in which every part swings at the same single frequency and the overall shape stays the same, only growing and shrinking. Every small free vibration is a sum of modes. Wikipedia

Standing wave

A wave whose shape stays in place, such as a mode of a string. It can be seen as two equal waves traveling in opposite directions. Wikipedia

Node, antinode, nodal line

A node is a point of a standing wave that does not move; an antinode is a point that moves the most. Touching a string lightly at a node of a mode does not disturb that mode. On a drumhead or a plate, a mode stays still along whole curves, its nodal lines; Chladni’s sand collects on them. Wikipedia

Wave equation

The equation u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} for the height u(x, t) of a stretched string, and its relatives for air in a pipe and for a drumhead. The constant c is the speed at which a bump travels. Wikipedia, and page 3

Boundary condition

A rule for what happens at the edge of a vibrating object, set by how it is held. A string tied down at an end has u = 0 there. A bar clamped at an end can neither move nor tilt there: u = 0 and u_x = 0. At the open end of a pipe the pressure equals room pressure. Wikipedia, and page 4

Dirichlet and Neumann conditions

Two kinds of boundary condition. A Dirichlet condition fixes the value at the edge, such as u = 0 at a string’s tied end or p = 0 at a pipe’s open end. A Neumann condition fixes the slope, such as p_x = 0 at a clarinet’s reed end. Wikipedia: Dirichlet, Neumann

Damping

Friction that drains energy from a vibration, so that it dies away. A term b\,u_t in the equation, proportional to velocity, is the simplest model. Wikipedia

Self-sustained oscillation, limit cycle

An oscillation kept going at a steady size by a steady supply of energy, such as a bow drawn at constant speed or a steady breath. In normal playing the motion settles into one repeating cycle, called a limit cycle; under some conditions it does not, as in the unsteady, warbling wolf note of some cellos. This needs a mechanism that is not linear, such as the bow’s grip and slip or a reed opening and closing. Wikipedia

Coupling

Two vibrating parts are coupled when the motion of one pushes on the other, as when piano strings share a bridge. Coupled parts trade energy, and their modes mix. Wikipedia

Helmholtz motion

The way a bowed string moves. The string sticks to the bow, slips back, and sticks again; seen from the side, a single sharp corner races back and forth along the string, one round trip per period. J. Wolfe, UNSW: The bowed string

Cantilever, clamped bar

A bar fixed rigidly at one end, so that end can neither move nor tilt, and free at the other, like a diving board. A kalimba tine is close to a cantilever: it is pressed against a bridge near one end and its tip is free. Wikipedia

Euler–Bernoulli beam

The standard model of a bending bar under no tension: \mu u_{tt} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}, where \mu is the mass per unit length, E the Young’s modulus and I the second moment of area. The bar resists being bent, and bending is curvature, two derivatives; balancing forces along the bar adds two more, giving four. Wikipedia

Bending moment, shear force

Imagine cutting a bent bar at some point. The bending moment is the turning effect that one side exerts on the other, which tries to bend the bar; the shear force is the sideways force across the cut. A free end carries neither. Wikipedia: Bending moment, Shear force

Young’s modulus

How stiff a material is when stretched: the force per unit area needed, divided by the fraction by which it lengthens. Steel is about 200 GPa; nylon, used for classical guitar strings, is a few GPa. Wikipedia

Second moment of area

How the shape of a bar’s cross-section resists bending, written I. For a rectangle of width w and thickness h, I = wh^3/12: doubling the thickness makes the bar eight times harder to bend. Wikipedia

Hyperbolic functions, cosh and sinh

\cosh x = (e^x + e^{-x})/2 and \sinh x = (e^x - e^{-x})/2. They satisfy \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1, much as \cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1. In a bar they describe the part of the bending that grows or fades along the bar instead of wiggling. Wikipedia

Bulk modulus, adiabatic

How hard a material is to compress: the pressure needed, divided by the fraction by which the volume shrinks. In a sound wave the squeezes are too quick for heat to flow in or out, which is called adiabatic, and for air this gives about 1.4 \times atmospheric pressure. Wikipedia

First-order approximation

Keeping only the terms proportional to a small change and dropping those proportional to its square and higher powers. For a small \varepsilon, (1 + \varepsilon)^3 = 1 + 3\varepsilon + 3\varepsilon^2 + \varepsilon^3 \approx 1 + 3\varepsilon to first order. A second-order approximation keeps the \varepsilon^2 terms too. Wikipedia

title: Glossary
text:
Matrices and operators

Matrix times vector

For a square matrix K and a list of numbers v, the product Kv is the list whose j-th entry is \sum_k K_{jk}v_k: row j of K, multiplied entry by entry with v and added up. Wikipedia

Eigenvector, eigenvalue

A nonzero vector v that a matrix K only rescales, multiplying it by a number \lambda: Kv = \lambda v. The number \lambda is the eigenvalue. On the bead ring of page 2, v lists how far each bead is displaced and Kv the forces pulling them back, up to a constant; an eigenvector is a shape in which each bead is pulled back in proportion to its own displacement, so all the beads swing at one frequency. Eigenvalues are squared angular frequencies, up to a constant. Wikipedia

Eigenvalue

See eigenvector.

Multiplicity

The number of independent eigenvectors that share one eigenvalue. Vectors are independent when none of them is a combination of the others. On a ring, the cosine and sine shapes of the same wave are two independent modes with the same frequency, so that frequency has multiplicity 2. Wikipedia

Perpendicular, orthogonal

Two vectors are perpendicular, or orthogonal, when their dot product, the sum of the products of matching entries, is zero. For functions the dot product is replaced by the inner product. Wikipedia

Symmetric matrix

A square matrix of real numbers equal to its own mirror image across the diagonal: the entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. The spectral theorem says its eigenvalues are real and it has a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors. Wikipedia

Determinant

A number computed from a square matrix that is zero exactly when the matrix sends some nonzero vector to zero. So linear equations with all right-hand sides zero have a solution other than all zeros exactly when the determinant of their coefficients is zero. For a 2\times2 matrix with rows (p, q) and (r, s) it is ps - qr. Wikipedia

Circulant matrix

A square matrix in which each row is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around. Whatever its entries, the complex waves e^{2\pi ijk/N} of the discrete Fourier transform, the next entry, are eigenvectors of it; when the matrix is also symmetric, as on page 2, so are the real cosine and sine waves. Wikipedia

Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)

Writing a list of N numbers, indexed by j = 0, \dots, N-1, as a sum of the waves \cos(2\pi jk/N) and \sin(2\pi jk/N) for k = 0, \dots, N-1; with Euler’s formula these are combined into e^{2\pi ijk/N}. Wikipedia, and page 2

Euler’s formula

e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta, where i^2 = -1. It packs a cosine and a sine into one expression that is easier to multiply and differentiate. Wikipedia

Operator

A rule that takes a function and returns another function. In this series the operator A takes a shape u of the instrument and returns minus the restoring force on it, per unit mass, so that the motion obeys u_{tt} = -Au. It comes with its allowed shapes, those that obey the boundary conditions. All of these operators are linear. Example: A = -c^2\,d^2/d\theta^2 on shapes of a loop. Pages 3 and 4 drop the constant c^2 and work with -d^2/d\theta^2, whose eigenvalues \lambda give frequencies c\sqrt\lambda/2\pi. Wikipedia

Eigenfunction

A nonzero function f that an operator only rescales: Af = \lambda f. Example: -\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\cos 3\theta = 9\cos 3\theta. Wikipedia

Spectrum

For every instrument in this series, the list of its operator’s eigenvalues; the frequencies are their square roots divided by 2\pi (when the constant c^2 is dropped from the operator, multiply by c too). (In general, for an operator on an infinite-dimensional space, the spectrum is the set of numbers \lambda for which A - \lambda has no well-behaved inverse, which can contain more than eigenvalues.) Wikipedia

Inner product

A way to multiply two vectors or two functions to get a number, generalizing the dot product. For functions on the circle, \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,\bar g\,d\theta, where \bar g is the complex conjugate of g, which is just g when g is real. Two functions are perpendicular if it is zero. Wikipedia

L^2(S^1)

The space of functions on the circle S^1 with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta finite, with the inner product above. (For readers who know measure theory: two functions that differ only on a set of measure zero count as the same.) It is where the shapes of a vibrating loop live. Wikipedia

Symmetric and self-adjoint operators

An operator A is symmetric if \langle Af, g\rangle = \langle f, Ag\rangle for all allowed f and g, the analogue of a symmetric matrix. That alone makes its eigenvalues real and its eigenfunctions for different eigenvalues perpendicular. Self-adjoint is a stronger condition on the set of allowed shapes, roughly that it is neither too small nor too large. Together with a further property that every instrument here has, it is what the spectral theorem needs to give enough eigenfunctions to build every shape (page 3). (For readers who know functional analysis: self-adjoint means A = A^*, domains included; for the loop the domain is H^2(S^1), and the further property is that (A + 1)^{-1} is compact.) Wikipedia

Fourier series

Writing a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines, or of e^{in\theta}, of whole-number frequencies. On page 3 this is the expansion in eigenfunctions of -d^2/d\theta^2. Wikipedia

Laplacian

The operator \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} in the plane. At each point it is proportional to how far u sits below the average of its values on a small circle around the point. A drumhead’s operator is -c^2\Delta. Wikipedia

Separation of variables

Looking for solutions that are a product of a function of one variable and a function of another, such as u(x, t) = X(x)\,q(t). It splits one equation in several variables into simpler equations in one variable each. Wikipedia

Bessel function

The functions J_m(r) that describe how the modes of a round drum vary from the center to the rim, as sines do along a string. J_0 starts at 1 and swings like a slowly fading cosine, crossing zero at r \approx 2.405,\ 5.520,\ 8.654, \dots; for m \ge 1, J_m starts at 0. Their zeros, which are not whole-number multiples of the first one, set the drum’s frequencies. Wikipedia, and page 8

Divergence theorem

The total flow out through the boundary of a region equals the sum, over the region, of how much flow is created at each point. It turns forces along the edge of a patch of drumhead into an integral over the patch. Wikipedia

Rayleigh quotient

The ratio of a shape’s stored energy to its mass-weighted size, for example R(f) = \int EI\,(f'')^2\,dx \big/ \int \rho S\,f^2\,dx for a bar; for a shape that meets all the boundary conditions it equals \langle Af, f\rangle/\langle f, f\rangle. Its smallest value, over all nonzero shapes f that obey the conditions at clamped or fixed ends, is the lowest eigenvalue, reached at the lowest mode; in this energy form, conditions at free ends need not be imposed. It explains why removing metal near the base of a reed or tine lowers its pitch and removing it near the tip raises it. Wikipedia

text:
Shape and spectrum

Weyl’s law

For a drum of area A, the number N(\lambda) of eigenvalues below a large number \lambda is close to A\lambda/4\pi, so the spectrum “hears” the area. A second term, -P\sqrt\lambda/4\pi with P the perimeter, is proved only under extra conditions, but for drums with smooth or polygonal rims the perimeter can be heard anyway, by a smoother count (page 9). Wikipedia

Isospectral

Having the same spectrum, counted with multiplicity. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert found two differently shaped drums that are isospectral. Wikipedia: Hearing the shape of a drum
