title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
How it works
A tine resists bending. A string is held straight by tension. A tine is under no tension at all: it springs back because steel resists being bent. That one change, bending instead of stretching, is behind both of the tine’s surprises below, through one fact: squeeze a shape into half the length, and a string pulls it back 4 times harder, but a tine pushes it back 16 times harder. Why 4 and 16? Squeezing a shape into half the length doubles every rate of change along it. A string’s pull depends on its curvature, how sharply it bends: a rate of change of a rate of change, 2 × 2 = 4. A tine’s push depends on how that curvature itself changes along the tine, twice over: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. (In the equation of motion, four derivatives where the string had two; the fold has the details.)



Step-by-step derivationThe tine’s equation: four derivatives instead of two uses partial derivatives and integrals over an area

Let u(x, t) be the tine’s height at distance x from the clamp at time t; subscripts are partial derivatives. A tine of Young’s modulus E (how stiff the steel is), cross-section area S, second moment of area I (how the cross-section’s shape resists bending) and density \rho obeys the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation 
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2\,u_{xxxx}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S}.
 Its operator is \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, where the string’s was -c^2\,d^2/dx^2. Two of the four derivatives measure how sharply the tine is bent, its curvature u_{xx}; the steel answers with a turning effect, the bending moment, proportional to it. One more turns the change of bending moment along the tine into the sideways force across each cut, the shear force, and the last turns the change of shear force along the tine into the net force on each piece.
Why 1/L^2. Take a tine twice as long, with the same cross-section; its mode shapes stretch to twice the length. Each of the four derivatives along the tine is then half as large, so the restoring force on the same shape is 2^4 = 16 times weaker, while the mass per unit length is unchanged. Frequency goes as the square root of force over mass, so it drops by a factor of 4: frequency goes as 1/L^2. For a string, two derivatives give 2^2 = 4 and a factor of 2: frequency as 1/L.
The derivation, step by step:


    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MM + dM
      VV + dV
      dx
    
    One slice of the tine. Bending moments (warm), the turning effects that bend it; shear forces (cool), the sideways forces across each cut, push it up and down. Torque balance links them; force balance moves the slice.
  

1. Bending stresses. Bend the bar. Fibers on the outside of the curve stretch and fibers on the inside compress, while a middle line, the neutral axis, keeps its length.

  
  
  
  
  stretched (y > 0)compressed (y < 0)
  neutral axis, y = 0

A fiber at height y above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction -y\,u_{xx} (for a gentle bend, the fraction by which a fiber stretches is its distance from the neutral axis times how fast the bar turns per unit length, which is the curvature u_{xx}), and by Hooke’s law it carries the stress (force per area) \sigma = -E\,y\,u_{xx}. Summed over the cross-section these forces cancel, which is what places the neutral axis through the middle (the centroid) of the cross-section, but their torques do not. They add up to the bending moment 
M = -\int_S y\,\sigma\,dA = E\,u_{xx}\int_S y^2\,dA = EI\,u_{xx}, \qquad I = \int_S y^2\,dA ,
 the integrals running over the cross-section. For a rectangle of width w and thickness h, I = wh^3/12; for a round wire of diameter d, I = \pi d^4/64.
2. Shear. A moment rotates a slice but cannot lift it. Each face of a slice also carries a vertical force, the shear force. The conventions: M is the moment on a face that bends the slice into an upward curve, counterclockwise on the right face and clockwise on the left; V is the upward force on the right face, and the left face feels the same force downward.

  
  
  
  
  
  
  MM + dM
  VV + dVdx

We neglect the slice’s resistance to being spun, its rotational inertia, which is accurate when the bar is thin compared with the length of its bending waves; then the torques on the slice must balance. Taking torques about the left face, the shear on the right face times the lever arm dx cancels the change in moment: V\,dx + dM = 0, so V = -M_x.
3. Newton’s law. The vertical forces on the slice do not balance: V(x + dx) - V(x) = V_x\,dx accelerates its mass \rho S\,dx. So \rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -M_{xx} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}, the equation above.
What was assumed. Small slopes, a uniform bar, no rotational inertia of the slices (Rayleigh’s correction for it adds a small term that matters only for thick bars and high modes), and no shear deformation of the slices (Timoshenko’s correction).


Half the length, two octaves up. A string half as long sounds an octave higher. A tine half as long sounds two octaves higher: its push-back grows 16 times instead of 4, and frequency goes as the square root of the push-back (page 1), so it rises 4 times instead of 2. A tine’s frequency goes as one over its length squared. That is why the low tines in the demo are not twice as long as the high ones an octave up. Kalimba makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge to change its free length (Kalimba Magic), and this makes a small slide go a long way.
Overtones off the lines. The same fact spreads the overtones out. Higher modes bend in shorter humps, and for a tine, shorter humps push back much harder, so the frequencies grow like the square of the mode number instead of the number itself. Where exactly they land depends on how the tine is held. Pinned at both ends, they would be 1, 4, 9, 16: whole numbers. Clamped at one end and free at the other, as a tine is, they are 1, 6.27, 17.55, …: off the whole numbers.



Step-by-step derivationWhere 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 comes from: the four end conditions uses hyperbolic functions, a 2×2 determinant and integration by parts

Boundary conditions. The bending moment is EI\,u_{xx} and the shear force is -EI\,u_{xxx} (the fold above derives both). At the base the tine is held down, so it can neither move nor tilt: u = 0 and u_x = 0. A bar held this way at one end and free at the other is called a cantilever. At the free tip nothing pushes or bends the bar, so both the moment and the shear force vanish: u_{xx} = 0 and u_{xxx} = 0. That is two conditions at each end, four in all.
Spectrum. Substituting a mode X(x)\cos\omega t into the equation gives \kappa^2 X'''' = \omega^2 X. Write \omega/\kappa = \beta^2, so that X'''' = \beta^4 X; the number \beta plays the role of the string’s wavenumber. Four functions solve this equation: \cos\beta x, \sin\beta x, \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x, where \cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2 and \sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2 are the hyperbolic functions. So X is a combination of the four with four unknown constants. The four boundary conditions are four equations for those constants, and they have a solution other than all zeros exactly when 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1 .
 The roots are \beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548,\ 10.9955, \dots, close to (n - \tfrac12)\pi from the second one on. Since \omega \propto \beta^2, the frequency ratios are 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39 : \cdots, growing like (2n-1)^2. With pinned ends, held in place but free to pivot, so u = u_{xx} = 0 at both ends, the shapes \sin(n\pi x/L) satisfy the conditions, four derivatives multiply them by (n\pi/L)^4, and the ratios are 1 : 4 : 9 : 16. The later roots sit near (n - \tfrac12)\pi; if all of them did, the ratios would be the whole numbers 1 : 9 : 25. The clamp and the free tip shift the first root most: it is 1.8751, not \pi/2 \approx 1.571.
Deriving the condition.

Clamped base. X(0) = 0 and X'(0) = 0 leave X = a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) + b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x).
Free tip. Differentiating, and dropping the common factors \beta^2 and \beta^3, the conditions X''(L) = 0 and X'''(L) = 0 read, with the shorthand C_1 = \cos\beta L, S_1 = \sin\beta L, C_2 = \cosh\beta L, S_2 = \sinh\beta L: 
-(C_1 + C_2)\,a - (S_1 + S_2)\,b = 0, \qquad (S_1 - S_2)\,a - (C_1 + C_2)\,b = 0 .

Nonzero solution. Two equations pa + qb = 0 and ra + sb = 0 have a solution other than a = b = 0 exactly when ps - qr = 0, the determinant: solve the first for a and substitute into the second. Here 
(C_1 + C_2)^2 + (S_1 + S_2)(S_1 - S_2) = C_1^2 + S_1^2 + 2C_1C_2 + C_2^2 - S_2^2 = 2 + 2C_1C_2 = 0,
 using C_1^2 + S_1^2 = 1 and C_2^2 - S_2^2 = 1. So \cos\beta L\cosh\beta L = -1.
Roots. Since \cosh\beta L grows fast, \cos\beta L must be close to 0, so \beta L \approx (n - \tfrac12)\pi, and the approximation improves quickly with n. The first root, 1.8751, is the furthest from it.

The operator d^4/dx^4 with these four conditions is symmetric, by integrating by parts four times (the boundary terms all vanish), so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenfunctions perpendicular, as on the circle; with the right domain it is also self-adjoint. Integrating by parts twice gives \int_0^L X\,X''''\,dx = \int_0^L (X'')^2\,dx, so no eigenvalue is negative, and zero is ruled out because X'' = 0 with a clamped base forces X = 0. That is why \beta is a real, positive number.


Why the note still sounds clean. You might guess the overtone is too quiet to hear. It isn’t. In how far the tine swings, the overtone is tiny; but the body hears the push on the bridge, not the swing, and in that push the overtone starts strong (fold below). That strong start is the click at the beginning of each note. What keeps the note clean is that the overtone dies within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on. Why it dies so fast is not computed here; the page takes it from measurement. The acoustician D. M. F. Chapman found exactly this pattern on a real kalimba: one dominant overtone, at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, gone soon after the attack.



Step-by-step derivationHow strongly a pluck at the tip excites each mode uses integration by parts

Chapman measured the tines of one kalimba, a Hugh Tracey pentatonic, and found one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, near the ideal 6.27, dying away quickly after the attack. A real tine is clamped a little behind the bridge and rests on the bridge partway along, rather than being perfectly clamped at one point, and he found that the measured ratios depend on how the bridge divides the tine’s length, which is one reason they spread. The steps below compute, for the ideal tine, how much of each mode a pluck starts. In short: in displacement, the second mode starts at only 2.5% of the first; but at the clamp, where in this ideal model the tine presses on the bridge, it starts at about 16% of the first in bending moment and 55% in shear force. Those are two different measures of the push on the bridge, not a range of uncertainty.

The pluck shape. Before release, a push F at the tip holds the tine still in a bent shape u_0, so the bar’s restoring force balances the push.
Split it into modes. Write u_0 = \sum_n c_n X_n, with each mode scaled so that \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L. Inside the tine nothing pushes, so EI\,u_0'''' = 0 there; the push enters only at the tip, as the shear force there. Now compute \int_0^L EI\,u_0\,X_n''''\,dx in two ways. First, EI\,X_n'''' = \rho S\,\omega_n^2X_n (the mode equation), and the modes are perpendicular, so only the c_n term survives: the integral is \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,c_n. Second, integrate by parts four times to move the derivatives onto u_0, as in the fold above. Inside, EI\,u_0'''' = 0; at the clamp both u_0 and X_n vanish with their slopes; at the tip X_n'' = X_n''' = 0 and u_0'' = 0. The one term left is the tip’s shear force times X_n(L), which is F\,X_n(L). So \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,c_n = F\,X_n(L). This is page 1’s spring again: mode n is a spring of stiffness proportional to \omega_n^2, pushed with a force proportional to its value at the tip, and it gives way by force over stiffness.
Tip values. Taking a = -1 and b = \sigma_n in the fold above gives the standard form X_n = \cosh\beta_nx - \cos\beta_nx - \sigma_n(\sinh\beta_nx - \sin\beta_nx), with \sigma_n = (\sinh\beta_nL - \sin\beta_nL)/(\cosh\beta_nL + \cos\beta_nL), about 0.734 and 1.018 for the first two modes. Written this way, each mode already has \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L, and its tip value is \pm2 for every n (a known property of clamped–free modes, easily confirmed numerically). So c_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2, and c_2/c_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%.
Forces. In this model the tine is clamped right at the bridge, so the forces at the clamp are the forces on the bridge. The bending moment at the clamp is EI\,u_{xx} there, and the shear force EI\,u_{xxx} there (up to sign). From the standard form, X_n''(0) = 2\beta_n^2 and X_n'''(0) = -2\sigma_n\beta_n^3. Multiplying by c_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2 \propto 1/\beta_n^4, the second mode’s moment at the clamp is (\beta_1/\beta_2)^2 = (1.875/4.694)^2 \approx 16\% of the first’s, and its shear force (\sigma_2/\sigma_1)(\beta_1/\beta_2) \approx 1.39 \times 0.40 \approx 55\%.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
What we found
On the pitch ruler, a kalimba tine’s frequencies are off the lines, so by the series’ rule it should clang. It doesn’t, because the off-line overtones die almost at once and leave one frequency ringing. Along the way, the tine taught two things: because shorter humps push back so much harder, its frequencies grow like the square of the mode number, and the way the ends are held decides whether they land on whole numbers.

Same math elsewhere. Harmonica reeds and the steel comb of a music box are also bars held at one end and free at the other.

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
The pitch ruler
The stems under the wave are the note’s frequencies, drawn as multiples of 220 Hz: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. Those whole-number multiples are the lines of the pitch ruler, and every page of this series puts an instrument on it. A note’s frequencies sit on the lines. Take away the 1× stem and the rest still sit on lines of the same ruler, so the pitch is still 220 Hz. The component at the repetition rate itself is called the fundamental. Hearing the pitch without it is called the missing fundamental effect, and it is why a deep voice keeps its pitch over an ordinary telephone line, which cannot carry sounds below about 300 Hz.
Open “Mix your own” and try the presets. The stems’ heights change, and so does the sound’s color, its timbre, but the pitch stays put as long as the base frequency does. Keep only 2×, 4×, 6× and 8×, and the sound repeats twice as often: the base becomes 440 Hz, and the pitch jumps up an octave.

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
How it works
A note is a pattern that repeats. Sound is air pressure rising and falling. When the pattern repeats, you hear a note, and its pitch is the repetition rate, measured in hertz. This holds for rates in the range where we hear pitch, from a few dozen to a few thousand times a second (for a recognizable melody, roughly 30 Hz to 4 or 5 kHz: Pressnitzer and colleagues measured the lower limit; the upper one is the traditional limit, which Oxenham and colleagues revisit). Much slower repetition is heard as a rhythm. Middle C, called C4, repeats about 262 times a second.
Every repeating sound is a chord on the lines. A pure tone is a single sine-shaped wave, the sound of a tuning fork. Any repeating pattern can be built from pure tones at 1, 2, 3, … times its repetition rate, and from no others; this is Fourier’s theorem, and page 3 shows where it comes from. These tones are the sound’s partials, and the one at the repetition rate itself is the fundamental. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not the fundamental is actually there; the partials’ strengths set the timbre.



PreciselyPeriodic signals and their Fourier series uses sums of cosines

Sound is a pressure signal p(t). It is periodic with period P if p(t + P) = p(t) for every t; take P to be the shortest such time. The pitch is the repetition rate f = 1/P, for rates in the range where we hear pitch.
Any periodic signal that is not too wild (continuous and made of smooth pieces is plenty) is the sum of its Fourier series, 
p(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} b_n \cos(2\pi n f t + \phi_n), \qquad f = 1/P .
 The n = 0 term is a constant, the average pressure, usually zero. The possible frequencies nf are fixed by the period alone, and a given sound may use only some of them: a pure tone uses only f. The amplitudes b_n and the phases \phi_n carry everything else about the sound’s shape, and the ear is mostly insensitive to the phases.





Reader questionIs a musical note one frequency?

No. A note is a sound whose pressure repeats every P seconds, and its pitch is the repetition rate f = 1/P. By the Fourier series above, its components can only be at f, 2f, 3f, \dots, and usually several are present at once. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not a component at f itself is present, and the weights b_n set the timbre: a piano C4 and a violin C4 share f and differ in their b_n. So a note corresponds to a period, not to a single frequency.


Why whole numbers matter. Turn it around. If something vibrates at several frequencies at once, its sound repeats only when they are all whole-number multiples of one common frequency. For two tones, the ratio of their frequencies must be a fraction, such as 3/2; the sound then repeats every 2 cycles of the lower tone. A ratio like 1.59, which is 159/100, repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch. Try it:


  ▶ 2 : 1▶ 3 : 2▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)Play the slider's ratio
  Ratio2.00×
  
  
  Gray ticks mark cycles of the lower tone. At 2 : 1 the sum repeats every cycle; at 3 : 2 every two; at 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, it lines up only after 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch.


Not every instrument is exact. Frequencies very near whole-number multiples still sound like one note: a piano’s are slightly off, as page 7 shows, and it still plays notes. So the rule this series tests every instrument against reads: frequencies at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch make a note.



ProofTwo tones repeat together exactly when their frequency ratio is a fraction uses cosines and divisibility

Let s(t) = \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + \cos(2\pi f_2 t) with 0 < f_1 < f_2.
If the ratio is rational, s is periodic. Write f_2/f_1 = j/k in lowest terms and put P = k/f_1. Then f_1P = k and f_2P = j are whole numbers, so both cosines return to their starting values after time P, and s(t+P) = s(t).
If s is periodic, the ratio is rational. Suppose s(t+P) = s(t) for all t, with P > 0. At t = 0 this gives s(P) = s(0) = 2. A sum of two cosines equals 2 only when both cosines equal 1, so \cos(2\pi f_1P) = \cos(2\pi f_2P) = 1, which means f_1P and f_2P are whole numbers. So f_2/f_1 = (f_2P)/(f_1P) is a ratio of whole numbers. Since f_2/f_1 = j/k, we have k\,(f_2P) = j\,(f_1P), so k divides j\,(f_1P); as j and k share no factor, k divides the whole number f_1P. So every period is a multiple of k/f_1, and k/f_1 is the shortest one.
The shortest period k/f_1 grows with the denominator k. A ratio like 1.59 = 159/100 is rational, but its pattern repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly for the ear to hear as one pitch. How the ear decides what counts as “simple enough”, and how near to whole-number multiples is near enough, are questions of perception, not mathematics; see pitch.

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
What we found
A note is a sound that repeats, and its pitch is how often it repeats. So a note’s frequencies sit on the lines of one pitch ruler, whole-number multiples of one base frequency, and that base frequency need not be present itself. Every later page puts an instrument on this ruler: on the lines, a note; off the lines, a clang or a thud.

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
text: Using a few examples, we demonstrate how to conditionally break out of nested for loop using for-else clause.

title: How to Break Nested For Loop
How to Break Nested For Loop
text:
2 Double Nested for Loop
Here, the program halts right after (i,j) reaches (2,1), which is what we want.

for i in range(4): # Layer 1
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3): # Layer 2
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: finished")
        continue # continuing for the enclosing for loop (layer 1), thus ignoring the "break"
    break # reached <=> continue was not called <=> for loop layer 2 was broken

Layer 1 for i = 0: start
  0 0
  0 1
  0 2
  Layer 2 for i = 0: finished
Layer 1 for i = 1: start
  1 0
  1 1
  1 2
  Layer 2 for i = 1: finished
Layer 1 for i = 2: start
  2 0
  2 1


Here, no continue in the else part. Thus, the program breaks unconditionally after finishing its job in the i==0 round.

for i in range(4):
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3):
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> the for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: completed")
    break # always reached at i = 0

  0 2
